Testing with testthat

This content was generated with the assistance of AI and should be verified against the official documentation before being relied on in production.

The reference material consulted while preparing these pages is listed in the section bibliography.

Checked against R 4.6.1 (2026-06-24) on 2026-10-20; R 4.6.2 is scheduled for 2026-10-29. This page uses the add-on package testthat 3.3.2 (the CRAN release of 2026-01-11) and the packages that go with it in the examples: withr 3.0.3 (temporary state), covr 3.6.5 (coverage), devtools 2.5.2 (the devtools::test() wrapper, which loads the package with pkgload 1.5.3), usethis 3.2.2 (calls to use_testthat() and use_test()), lintr 3.4.0 (one call to lint_package()), rlang 1.3.0 (one custom expectation calls rlang::enquo()) and tinytest 1.4.3 (one run of its test runner and one call to setup_tinytest()). testthat itself compares objects with waldo 0.6.2 and prints with cli 3.6.6; R CMD build rebuilt the vignette of the package with knitr 1.52 and rmarkdown 2.32. The shelf package is the one built for the Creating Packages page, version 0.1.0. The package DT, which covr::report() needs, is not installed in the image used here, so that one call is shown failing and nothing else is claimed about its output. A GitHub Actions workflow is shown as a fragment that was not run, and Codecov is only named.

Testing is the habit of writing down what a piece of code is supposed to do as code that checks it, so that the checking can be repeated after every change. R itself ships only the minimal machinery for this: the tests directory of a package, whose .R files R CMD check runs, with optional reference output next to them. Almost every package on CRAN goes through testthat instead, an add-on package that gives that directory a structure: a test is a named block, a test contains expectations, expectations say what the result must look like and produce readable failure reports, and a few special files hold shared helpers and fixtures. This page explains that structure with the tests of the shelf package, the tools that run and report them, the features around them (snapshots, mocking, skipping, fixtures, the third edition), and the base-R and tinytest alternatives. It ends with coverage measurement with covr and a CI fragment.

Every example is a script that was run with Rscript on R 4.6.1 with warnings printed as they happen (options(warn = 1)), and the lines that start with #> are what it printed. The scripts also pass the default lintr linters (whose line limit is 80 characters). The names books, loans and shelf_today and the book() constructor come from the running library-shelf scenario described on the section index: a script that needs them starts with source("scenario.R"), or calls shelf:: functions when the built package is used. The shelf package shown here was created, documented, tested, built and checked for real with these tools; its files are shown as the tools wrote them. The experiments that change the package (a failing test file, a changed print method, a parallel setting) ran in a throwaway copy of the package directory and each one puts everything back; the transcripts show the package path as ~/shelf (paths shortened). The default testthat reporters finish a passing run with a random emoji or a short word of praise, and print a spinner line that a terminal overwrites in place but that a captured log keeps as separate lines. The scripts therefore silence the praise where they can (StopReporter$new(praise = FALSE)), and the few transcripts that still contain a random line say which one was left out.

This page builds on Creating Packages, which made the package, and on Documentation with Rd, roxygen2 and Vignettes; the conditions that expect_error() and its relatives catch are explained in Conditions and Error Handling, and the checks a function should make of its own arguments in Defensive Programming and Input Validation. Style checking of the tests is the subject of Style, Linting and Static Analysis, and running the whole check before a release of Publishing to CRAN.

Where tests live and how testthat fits

A package keeps its tests in the tests directory, which Writing R Extensions describes as the place for package-specific test code: .R files whose results are written to a .Rout file, which R CMD check compares with a .Rout.save file when one exists. The directory is copied to the check area, the tests run with that copy as the working directory, in a vanilla R session without a random-number seed, with R_LIBS set so that library(shelf) finds the copy of the package installed for the check. R does not say how the tests should be written. testthat is a convention on top of that mechanism, and a package opts in with three things: Suggests: testthat in DESCRIPTION (a package used only to run tests is a suggestion, not an import), a one-line driver in tests/testthat.R, and the test files in tests/testthat/.

Source: Writing R Extensions: Package subdirectories

The vocabulary has four levels, and the names matter because the failure reports and the reporters use them.

Level What it is Where it is written

Expectation

One check of one result: expect_equal(x, y). It succeeds, fails, or is skipped, and reports what it saw.

a call of an expect_*() function

Test

A named group of expectations that share local objects and are reported together.

test_that("description", { ... }) or it("description", { ... })

File

The tests of one source file or one topic; the unit that snapshots, filters and the progress display work on.

tests/testthat/test-*.R

Suite

Every file, plus the helper and setup files that prepare them.

tests/testthat/, run by test_check(), devtools::test() or test_local()

Source: testthat package documentation: test_that

Each test runs in a fresh environment whose parent is the package namespace when the tests belong to a package, so a test can call internal functions such as shelf_today() without :::. The expectations are ordinary functions that signal an expectation condition; the reporter listening for those conditions counts them and prints the failures. Because a test is just code that runs in a controlled environment, everything the other pages teach about functions, scoping and conditions applies inside it.

The layout of the tests directory

tests/testthat.R

usethis::use_testthat(3) creates the directory and the driver. The script below runs it on a throwaway package in a temporary directory (not on shelf, which already has the result) and prints the messages of the call, the files that exist afterwards, the driver it wrote and the two lines of DESCRIPTION that mention testthat:

# A throwaway package in a temporary directory (nothing of shelf is touched).
dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "tmpkg")
invisible(capture.output(
  suppressMessages(usethis::create_package(dir, open = FALSE))
))

# Keep the messages of use_testthat(), without the line that names the path.
msgs <- character()
withCallingHandlers(
  usethis::with_project(dir, usethis::use_testthat(3)),
  message = \(m) {
    msgs <<- c(msgs, conditionMessage(m))
    invokeRestart("muffleMessage")
  }
)
cat(grep("active project", msgs, value = TRUE, invert = TRUE), sep = "")
#> ✔ Adding testthat to 'Suggests' field in DESCRIPTION.
#> ✔ Adding "3" to 'Config/testthat/edition'.
#> ✔ Creating 'tests/testthat/'.
#> ✔ Writing 'tests/testthat.R'.
#> ☐ Call `usethis::use_test()` to initialize a basic test file and open it for
#>   editing.

list.files(dir, recursive = TRUE)
#> [1] "DESCRIPTION"      "NAMESPACE"        "tests/testthat.R"
cat(readLines(file.path(dir, "tests", "testthat.R")), sep = "\n")
#> # This file is part of the standard setup for testthat.
#> # It is recommended that you do not modify it.
#> #
#> # Where should you do additional test configuration?
#> # Learn more about the roles of various files in:
#> # * https://r-pkgs.org/testing-design.html#sec-tests-files-overview
#> # * https://testthat.r-lib.org/articles/special-files.html
#>
#> library(testthat)
#> library(tmpkg)
#>
#> test_check("tmpkg")
grep("testthat", readLines(file.path(dir, "DESCRIPTION")), value = TRUE)
#> [1] "    testthat (>= 3.0.0)"    "Config/testthat/edition: 3"

Source: usethis package documentation: use_testthat

The argument 3 selects the third edition of testthat (see The third edition), which the call records in DESCRIPTION. The fragment of the DESCRIPTION of shelf that matters for testing is:

Suggests:
    knitr,
    rmarkdown,
    testthat (>= 3.0.0),
    withr
Config/testthat/edition: 3
Depends:
    R (>= 4.1.0)

Source: Writing R Extensions: Package Dependencies

The Suggests field lists the packages that tests, examples and vignettes use but that the package does not need in order to work; withr is there because the tests call withr::local_options() with ::, and testthat (>= 3.0.0) is the version that introduced the third edition. Writing R Extensions says that a package used by tests must be listed in Depends, Imports or Suggests, that code using a suggested package must be conditional on it being there, and that this includes the packages that manage test suites; its example is testthat 1.0.0, which once contained code that did not compile on standards-compliant platforms. testthat 3.3.0 took one half of this burden off the test authors: on CRAN, test_that() now skips a test automatically when a package that the test needs is not installed.

Source: Writing R Extensions: Suggested packages

The list is checked. With the line testthat (>= 3.0.0), deleted from Suggests and R CMD check --as-cran run on the result (the output is trimmed to the lines about the tests), the check reports the undeclared dependency. --as-cran also turns on _R_CHECK_SUGGESTS_ONLY_, which R Internals documents as true for the CRAN submission checks and which runs examples, tests and vignettes with a temporary library holding only the declared packages, so the run then fails at the first line of tests/testthat.R:

* checking for unstated dependencies in ‘tests’ ... WARNING
'library' or 'require' call not declared from: ‘testthat’
* checking tests ...
  Running ‘testthat.R’
 ERROR
Running the tests in ‘tests/testthat.R’ failed.
Complete output:
  > # This file is part of the standard setup for testthat.
  > # It is recommended that you do not modify it.
  > #
  > # Where should you do additional test configuration?
  > # Learn more about the roles of various files in:
  > # * https://r-pkgs.org/testing-design.html#sec-tests-files-overview
  > # * https://testthat.r-lib.org/articles/special-files.html
  >
  > library(testthat)
  Error in library(testthat) : there is no package called 'testthat'
  Execution halted

Status: 1 ERROR, 1 WARNING

Source: R Internals: Tools

The file tests/testthat.R is what R CMD check actually runs. This is the file use_testthat() wrote, unchanged:

# This file is part of the standard setup for testthat.
# It is recommended that you do not modify it.
#
# Where should you do additional test configuration?
# Learn more about the roles of various files in:
# * https://r-pkgs.org/testing-design.html#sec-tests-files-overview
# * https://testthat.r-lib.org/articles/special-files.html

library(testthat)
library(shelf)

test_check("shelf")

Source: testthat package documentation: test_check

library(testthat) attaches the expectation functions and library(shelf) the package being tested (the same call that prints the startup message shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days); test_check("shelf") then finds tests/testthat/ relative to the check directory, runs every file in it with the check reporter and, if anything failed, ends with an error that makes R CMD check report the test run as failed. The comment header, which testthat says not to modify, points to the article on the special files. Everything else about the suite goes into tests/testthat/, not into this file.

tests/testthat/

The files in tests/testthat/ have different jobs, decided by their names. Only names matter, not contents:

File or directory Role

test-*.R (or test_*.R, extension .R or .r)

Test files. Run in alphabetical order; each should pass when run alone or in any order. The convention is one test file for each file in R/: R/loans.R has tests/testthat/test-loans.R, and usethis::use_test() and devtools::test_active_file() rely on that correspondence.

helper-*.R

Helper code: functions and constants shared by the tests, custom expectations, skip helpers. Sourced by devtools::load_all() and by test_check() and its relatives, so the helpers exist however the tests are run.

setup-*.R (by convention setup.R)

Global preparation for a run, such as turning off interactive behaviour. Sourced by test_check() and friends but not by load_all(). Cleanup belongs next to the setup with withr::defer(..., teardown_env()).

teardown-*.R

The legacy place for cleanup, no longer recommended. Run after the tests.

fixtures/ (any name)

Data files for the tests. Files that testthat does not know are ignored by it, which makes the directory a safe place for persistent test data; reach it with test_path().

_snaps/

Snapshot files written and read by expect_snapshot() and friends, named after the test file; never edited by hand, always committed.

_problems/

Written in a check directory when a test fails under R CMD check (testthat 3.3.0): one reprex file for each failing expectation.

Source: testthat package documentation: Special files

The listing of the tests directory of shelf, as find prints it (the order is the collation order of sort):

tests
tests/testthat
tests/testthat/fixtures
tests/testthat/fixtures/books-small.csv
tests/testthat/helper-shelf.R
tests/testthat.R
tests/testthat/_snaps
tests/testthat/_snaps/book.md
tests/testthat/test-book.R
tests/testthat/test-clean.R
tests/testthat/test-loans.R

Source: testthat package documentation: Special files

usethis::use_test("name") creates tests/testthat/test-name.R with a one-test template and reports the file it wrote. The template for a name that does not match an existing file in R/ is:

usethis::with_project(
  ".",
  usethis::use_test("scratch", open = FALSE),
  quiet = TRUE
)
cat(readLines("tests/testthat/test-scratch.R"), sep = "\n")
unlink("tests/testthat/test-scratch.R")
#> test_that("multiplication works", {
#>   expect_equal(2 * 2, 4)
#> })

Source: usethis package documentation: use_test

The usethis::with_project(".", ..., quiet = TRUE) wrapper is only there so that the script prints the template and not usethis’s own messages. The script is a fragment to run from the package directory: it reads back the file that use_test() wrote and deletes it. In an interactive session the call is simply usethis::use_test("name"), and with the file R/name.R open usethis::use_test() picks the name itself.

The tests of the shelf package

The suite of shelf has three test files, one helper file and one fixture. They are package test files, run by devtools::test() or test_check(), not scripts to run with Rscript; the blocks below are the files exactly as they are in ~/shelf/tests/testthat/, and each is explained in the sections that follow. They pass the default lintr linters with one finding, explained below. Together they hold 52 expectations: devtools::test() reports [ FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 0 | PASS 52 ].

helper-shelf.R

The helper is loaded before every test file. It defines the one fixed date that the tests share and a function that reads the small catalogue fixture through test_path().

# Loaded before every test file: a fixed "today" and a helper that reads the
# small catalogue fixture.
shelf_fixed_today <- as.Date("2026-06-30")

read_fixture_books <- function() {
  read.csv(test_path("fixtures", "books-small.csv"))
}

Source: testthat package documentation: test_path

Linting this file in a fresh session finds one thing, and the reason is a general property of lintr and not a problem of the helper. object_usage_linter asks the R session which functions exist, and a plain Rscript -e 'lintr::lint_package()' has not attached testthat, so test_path() is "not visible". The recorded build of the package linted it after devtools::test() had attached testthat and found nothing. The second call below attaches testthat first:

# A fresh session does not know test_path(): lintr cannot see where it is from.
lintr::lint_package()

# With testthat attached the same file is clean.
library(testthat)
lintr::lint_package()

Source: lintr package documentation: lint_package

The first call prints the lint (the file, line and column, the linter and its message, the line of code and a marker under the name); the second prints the message No lints found.:

tests/testthat/helper-shelf.R:6:12: warning: [object_usage_linter] no visible global function definition for 'test_path'
  read.csv(test_path("fixtures", "books-small.csv"))
           ^~~~~~~~~
ℹ No lints found.

Source: lintr package documentation: lint_package

The remedies are testthat::test_path() called with the package name in the helper, or a # nolint: object_usage_linter. comment on the line, or listing testthat among the globals in .lintr; the file is shown as written.

test-book.R

The tests of the book class: normalising input, optional fields, the error messages of validate_book(), the type check of new_book(), two snapshot tests, and a describe() block for is_valid_isbn13().

test_that("book() trims the text fields and normalises the ISBN", {
  b <- book("  the quiet streets ", "Mara  Quill", "978-0-00-100010-0",
            "2019", "Fiction ", 214)
  expect_s3_class(b, "book")
  expect_identical(b$title, "the quiet streets")
  expect_identical(b$author, "Mara Quill")
  expect_identical(b$isbn, "9780001000100")
  expect_identical(b$year, 2019L)
  expect_identical(b$genre, "Fiction")
  expect_type(b$pages, "integer")
})

test_that("book() accepts missing optional fields", {
  b <- book("Untitled Draft")
  expect_true(is.na(b$author))
  expect_true(is.na(b$isbn))
  expect_identical(format(b), "Untitled Draft (NA, n.d.)")
})

test_that("validate_book() rejects bad values with a clear message", {
  expect_error(book(""), "a book needs a title")
  expect_error(book("X", isbn = "9780001000101"), "invalid ISBN-13")
  expect_error(book("X", year = 2200), "implausible year")
  expect_error(
    validate_book(new_book(title = c("a", "b"))),
    "every field of a book must have length 1"
  )
})

test_that("new_book() checks types only", {
  expect_error(new_book(title = 1), "is.character(title) is not TRUE",
               fixed = TRUE)
  b <- new_book(title = "x", author = "y", isbn = "z", year = 1L,
                genre = "g", pages = 2L)
  expect_identical(class(b), "book")
  expect_identical(class(unclass(b)), "list")
})

test_that("a book prints and summarises as expected", {
  b <- book("Salt and Static", "Mara Quill", "978-0-01-400145-3", 2018,
            "Mystery", 244)
  expect_snapshot(print(b))
  expect_snapshot(summary(b))
  expect_s3_class(summary(b), "summary.book")
  expect_output(print(book("Paper Moons", "Noor Haddad")), "n.d.")
})

describe("is_valid_isbn13()", {
  it("accepts hyphenated and bare forms of a valid ISBN", {
    expect_identical(
      is_valid_isbn13(c("978-0-00-100010-0", "9780001000100")),
      c(TRUE, TRUE)
    )
  })
  it("rejects wrong check digits, short strings, empty strings and NA", {
    expect_identical(
      is_valid_isbn13(c("9780001000101", "978030640615", "", NA)),
      c(FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE)
    )
  })
  it("returns a logical of the same length, including length zero", {
    expect_identical(is_valid_isbn13(character()), logical())
  })
})

The two snapshot expectations write their results to tests/testthat/_snaps/book.md, a file named after the test file and committed with the package:

    Code

    Output
      <book> Salt and Static (Mara Quill, 2018)

---

    Code

      ISBN known: TRUE

test_that("clean_books() keeps the shape of the packaged catalogue", {
  cleaned <- clean_books(books)
  expect_identical(dim(cleaned), dim(books))
  expect_identical(names(cleaned), names(books))

test_that("clean_loans() parses dates and repairs impossible values", {
  raw <- data.frame(
    loan_id = c("L1", "L2", "L3"),
    isbn = rep("9780001000100", 3L),
    member = c("Ana Ruiz", "ana  ruiz ", ""),
    loan_date = c("2026-01-10", "2026-02-30", "2026-03-01"),
    return_date = c("2026-01-05", "", "2026-03-20")
  )

test_that("clean_loans() leaves Date columns alone", {
  expect_identical(clean_loans(loans)$loan_date, loans$loan_date)
})

Source: testthat package documentation: expect_setequal

The fixture is a three-row catalogue with one row of every kind of mess that clean_books() repairs: a title with blanks and lower case, a hyphenated ISBN, an empty ISBN and a double space in an author. The expected values in the test are small enough to be written out, which is what makes the test a good specification. The third test builds its input in the test itself, as a three-row data frame, because the impossible date and the early return belong to the case being described and a reader should see them next to the expectation.

test-loans.R

The tests of the loan analyses use the shared fixed date, replace the package’s clock in one test, change an option in another and skip one test on CRAN.

test_that("overdue_loans() counts late returns and loans still out", {
  out <- overdue_loans(loans, today = shelf_fixed_today)
  expect_true(all(out$days_out > 21L))
  expect_identical(sum(is.na(out$return_date)), 7L)
  expect_identical(nrow(out), 32L)
  expect_false(any(is.na(out$loan_date)))
})

test_that("overdue_loans() uses the current date by default", {
  local_mocked_bindings(shelf_today = function() shelf_fixed_today)
  expect_identical(
    overdue_loans(loans),
    overdue_loans(loans, today = shelf_fixed_today)
  )
})

test_that("the loan period comes from the shelf.loan_days option", {
  withr::local_options(shelf.loan_days = 60L)
  out <- overdue_loans(loans, today = shelf_fixed_today)
  expect_true(all(out$days_out > 60L))
  expect_lt(nrow(out), 32L)
})

test_that("loan_summary() reports one row per genre", {
  cleaned <- clean_books(books)
  s <- loan_summary(loans, cleaned, today = shelf_fixed_today)
  expect_named(s, c("genre", "loans", "overdue", "overdue_rate"))
  expect_identical(s$genre, sort(unique(cleaned$genre)))
  expect_true(all(s$overdue <= s$loans))
  expect_equal(s$overdue_rate, s$overdue / s$loans)
})

test_that("loans_per_month() returns months in order", {
  m <- loans_per_month(loans)
  expect_identical(m$month, sort(m$month))
  expect_identical(sum(m$loans), sum(!is.na(loans$loan_date)))
})

test_that("a long check is skipped on CRAN", {
  skip_on_cran()
  big <- loans[rep(seq_len(nrow(loans)), 50L), ]
  expect_identical(
    nrow(overdue_loans(big, today = shelf_fixed_today)),
    32L * 50L
  )
})

Source: testthat package documentation: local_mocked_bindings

All of the tests use the packaged books and loans, which the package exports as lazy-loaded data, so no test reads a file from the working directory. That is deliberate: a test may not rely on the working directory, a network or the current date, which are the three things that differ between a laptop and a check machine.

A first test: test_that() and expectations

test_that(desc, code) takes a description and a block of code. The description should finish the sentence "test that …​": the failure report quotes it, and a suite of well-chosen descriptions reads as a specification. The block is evaluated in its own environment with the reporter listening: every expect_*() call inside it registers one result, a failed expectation does not stop the block (the later expectations still run and are reported), and an error that is not caught by an expectation ends the block and is reported as an error against the test. A block without any expectation is reported as skipped, with the reason empty test. test_that() also calls local_test_context(), which sets the environment variable TESTTHAT and, in the third edition, makes the output reproducible (see Reproducible output); it does not need a context() call.

A test file can also be run as a script, which is the easiest way to see the mechanics. Outside a package there is no DESCRIPTION to say which edition applies, so the scripts select the third edition with the environment variable TESTTHAT_EDITION (the third-edition section explains why). In a script, test_that() uses the stop reporter: a passing test prints nothing here (with praise on, it prints Test passed and a random emoji), and a failing test prints its report and then stops the script with an error, so the script catches it to go on.

library(testthat)
source("scenario.R")
set_reporter(StopReporter$new(praise = FALSE))

# A test is a description plus a block of expectations.
test_that("addition works", {
  expect_equal(1 + 1, 2)
  expect_true(is.numeric(1L))
})

# A test with a failing expectation stops the script; catch it to continue.
result <- tryCatch(
  test_that("a failing expectation", {
    expect_equal(1 + 1, 3)
  }),
  error = \(e) conditionMessage(e)
)
#> ── Failure: a failing expectation ──────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Expected `1 + 1` to equal 3.
#> Differences:
#> 1/1 mismatches
#> [1] 2 - 3 == -1
result
#> [1] "Test failed with 1 failure and 0 successes."

# An error inside the block is also reported against the test.
tryCatch(
  test_that("an error inside a test", {
    books$title[[100L]]
  }),
  error = \(e) conditionMessage(e)
)
#> ── Error: an error inside a test ───────────────────────────────────────────────
#> <subscriptOutOfBoundsError/error/condition>
#> Error in `books$title[[100L]]`: subscript out of bounds
#> [1] "Test failed with 1 failure and 0 successes."

# A test without expectations is skipped as empty.
test_that("nothing is checked here", {
  x <- 1 + 1
})
#> ── Skip: nothing is checked here ───────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Reason: empty test

Source: testthat package documentation: test_that

The report of the failure shows the three parts that every failure has: the location (here the test description; in a file, the file and line), the sentence that says what the expectation expected, and the differences. Since testthat 3.3.0 every expectation states what it expected and what it saw in the same shape, and returns the value of its first argument whether it succeeds or fails, so chains of expectations work, as the last line of the script in the section on types and classes shows.

The rest of this section goes through the families of expectations. Every example here is a script in which a failed expectation raises an error; the one-line helper failure() catches that error and prints its message, which is exactly the text that appears in a test report. An expectation that succeeds prints nothing.

Equality: expect_equal() and expect_identical()

expect_identical(object, expected) demands that the two objects are the same, the way identical() does for the base data types. expect_equal(object, expected) demands that they are the same up to numerical error: it differs from expect_identical() only in setting tolerance = testthat_tolerance(), so small floating-point differences are ignored, and as a consequence 1 and 1L are equal. Both compare with waldo::compare() in the third edition; in the second edition expect_identical() used identical() and expect_equal() used all.equal(), whose tolerance rules are different for different code paths. The tolerance is the one of all.equal(): relative to the size of the numbers, absolute when the differences are very small. The rule for choosing is simple. Use expect_identical() for what is exact by construction (strings, integers, logicals, names, classes, NA values) and expect_equal() for results of floating-point arithmetic. For the arithmetic itself, see Numbers and Arithmetic.

library(testthat)
Sys.setenv(TESTTHAT_EDITION = "3")
source("scenario.R")

# Outside test_that() a failed expectation is an error: catch it to read it.
failure <- \(code) tryCatch(code, error = \(e) cat(conditionMessage(e), "\n"))

# Floating point: equal within tolerance, but not identical.
x <- 0.1 + 0.2
expect_equal(x, 0.3)
failure(expect_identical(x, 0.3))
#> Expected `x` to be identical to 0.3.
#> Differences:
#>   `actual`: 0.300000000000000044
#> `expected`: 0.299999999999999989
#>

# Integer vs double: identical() is strict about the type.
expect_equal(2L, 2)
failure(expect_identical(2L, 2))
#> Expected 2L to be identical to 2.
#> Differences:
#> `actual` is an integer vector (2)
#> `expected` is a double vector (2)
#>

# The default tolerance is the one of all.equal(), and it is relative.
testthat_tolerance()
#> [1] 1.490116e-08
failure(expect_equal(100, 101))
#> Expected 100 to equal 101.
#> Differences:
#>   `actual`: 100.0
#> `expected`: 101.0
#>
expect_equal(100, 101, tolerance = 0.05)

# waldo describes where two objects differ.
b1 <- book("Salt and Static", "Mara Quill", year = 2018)
b2 <- book("Salt and Static", "Mara Quill", year = 2019)
failure(expect_equal(b1, b2))
#> Expected `b1` to equal `b2`.
#> Differences:
#>   `actual$year`: 2018
#> `expected$year`: 2019
#>

# Attributes and names matter unless you ignore them.
failure(expect_equal(c(a = 1, b = 2), c(1, 2)))
#> Expected `c(a = 1, b = 2)` to equal `c(1, 2)`.
#> Differences:
#> `names(actual)` is a character vector ('a', 'b')
#> `names(expected)` is absent
#>
expect_equal(c(a = 1, b = 2), c(1, 2), ignore_attr = TRUE)

# Two data frames of different length: every differing column is reported.
failure(expect_equal(head(books[, 1:3], 2), head(books[, 1:3], 3)))
#> Expected `head(books[, 1:3], 2)` to equal `head(books[, 1:3], 3)`.
#> Differences:
#>   `attr(actual, 'row.names')`: 1 2
#> `attr(expected, 'row.names')`: 1 2 3
#>
#> actual vs expected
#>                                title            author              isbn
#>   actual[1, ]   The Dispossessed     Ursula K. Le Guin 978-0-306-40615-7
#>   actual[2, ]   Pride and Prejudice  Jane Austen       978-0-14-143951-8
#> + expected[3, ]   the quiet streets  Mara Quill        9780001000100
#>
#>     actual$title          | expected$title
#> [1] "The Dispossessed"    | "The Dispossessed"     [1]
#> [2] "Pride and Prejudice" | "Pride and Prejudice"  [2]
#>                           - "  the quiet streets " [3]
#>
#> `actual$author`:   "Ursula K. Le Guin" "Jane Austen"
#> `expected$author`: "Ursula K. Le Guin" "Jane Austen" "Mara Quill"
#>
#> `actual$isbn`:   "978-0-306-40615-7" "978-0-14-143951-8"
#> `expected$isbn`: "978-0-306-40615-7" "978-0-14-143951-8" "9780001000100"
#>

Source: testthat package documentation: expect_equal and expect_identical

The waldo reports are the main reason to use the third edition. The report for b1 and b2 is actual$year against expected$year: it names the element that differs and shows both values. For a data frame with a row missing waldo prints a side-by-side table of the differing rows and then one comparison for each column that differs, which is more than the message all.equal() would give but still points at the first thing to look at. The extra arguments of expect_equal() go to waldo::compare(): ignore_attr = TRUE ignores attributes such as names (the old expect_equivalent()), and ignore_function_env and ignore_formula_env ignore the environments of functions and formulas, which differ between runs when tests compare fitted models.

Logical, type and class expectations

expect_true(x) and expect_false(x) require a single TRUE or FALSE, not something that merely behaves like one: expect_true(1) fails, because 1 is a double, and expect_true(c(TRUE, FALSE)) fails because the length is two. expect_null() checks NULL. The type and class expectations check the object system explicitly, which is why the older expect_is() is deprecated in the third edition: expect_type(x, "integer") checks typeof(), expect_s3_class(x, "book") checks that an S3 object inherits from a class (exact = TRUE requires the class vector to be exactly that), expect_s4_class() an S4 class, and expect_s7_class() and expect_r6_class() the S7 and R6 equivalents. Passing NA as the class asserts that the object is not an S3 (or S4) object at all. Two newer helpers check the shape in one call: expect_vector(x, ptype, size) and expect_shape(x, nrow, ncol, dim).

library(testthat)
Sys.setenv(TESTTHAT_EDITION = "3")
source("scenario.R")

failure <- \(code) tryCatch(code, error = \(e) cat(conditionMessage(e), "\n"))

# Logical expectations.
expect_true(is_valid_isbn13("978-0-306-40615-7"))
expect_false(is_valid_isbn13(""))
failure(expect_true(c(TRUE, FALSE)))
#> Expected `c(TRUE, FALSE)` to be TRUE.
#> Differences:
#> `actual`:   TRUE FALSE
#> `expected`: TRUE
#>
failure(expect_true(1))
#> Expected 1 to be TRUE.
#> Differences:
#> `actual` is a double vector (1)
#> `expected` is a logical vector (TRUE)
#>
expect_null(NULL)

# Types: the typeof() of the object.
b <- book("Salt and Static", "Mara Quill", year = 2018)
expect_type(b, "list")
expect_type(b$year, "integer")
failure(expect_type(b$year, "double"))
#> Expected `b$year` to have type "double".
#> Actual type: "integer"

# S3 classes: expect_s3_class() checks inherits(), exact = TRUE the whole class.
expect_s3_class(b, "book")
expect_s3_class(summary(b), "summary.book")
failure(expect_s3_class(b, "data.frame"))
#> Expected `b` to inherit from "data.frame".
#> Actual class: "book".
failure(expect_s3_class(unclass(b), "book"))
#> Expected `unclass(b)` to be an S3 object.
#> Actual OO type: none.
expect_s3_class(books, "data.frame")
expect_s3_class(books, "data.frame", exact = TRUE)
expect_s3_class(unclass(b), NA)

# S4 classes (and S7 with expect_s7_class()) have their own expectations.
setClass("Shelf", slots = c(books = "character"))
s <- new("Shelf", books = "A")
expect_s4_class(s, "Shelf")
failure(expect_s4_class(b, "Shelf"))
#> Expected `b` to be an S4 object.
#> Actual OO type: S3.

# The vector helpers check type, length and shape in one call.
expect_vector(books$year, ptype = integer(), size = nrow(books))
expect_shape(books, dim = c(16L, 6L))
failure(expect_shape(books, nrow = 20L))
#> Expected `books` to have 20 rows.
#> Actual rows: 16.

# Since testthat 3.3.0 an expectation returns its first argument: chain them.
books |> expect_s3_class("data.frame") |> expect_length(6L)

Source: testthat package documentation: expect_type and expect_s3_class

The class of b is "book", so expect_s3_class(b, "data.frame") fails and reports the actual class; the unclassed list is Actual OO type: none. See S3 Classes and Generics for what the class attribute is, and S4 Classes and Methods for setClass().

Length, names, sets, comparisons and text

These expectations exist because expect_equal(length(x), 6L) and expect_true(all(a %in% b)) fail with messages that say nothing about the objects. The dedicated forms say what they saw:

  • expect_length(x, n) and expect_named(x, names, ignore.order, ignore.case);

  • expect_setequal(x, y): the same elements, in any order and with any duplication; expect_mapequal(x, y): the same names and the same value for each name, in any order;

  • expect_contains(x, y): every element of y is in x, and expect_in(x, y): every element of x is in y (the two directions of subset, added in testthat 3.1.9); expect_disjoint() the opposite;

  • expect_lt(), expect_lte(), expect_gt() and expect_gte() compare numbers, dates and times, and show both values on failure;

  • expect_match(x, regexp) and expect_no_match() match text against a regular expression (see Strings and Regular Expressions), and expect_all_true(), expect_all_false() and expect_all_equal() check every element at once (testthat 3.3.0) and say which elements differ, where expect_true(all(...)) can only say FALSE.

library(testthat)
Sys.setenv(TESTTHAT_EDITION = "3")
source("scenario.R")

failure <- \(code) tryCatch(code, error = \(e) cat(conditionMessage(e), "\n"))

genres <- unique(tolower(trimws(books$genre)))

# Length and names.
expect_length(books, 6L)
failure(expect_length(genres, 5L))
#> Expected `genres` to have length 5.
#> Actual length: 6.
expect_named(books, c("title", "author", "isbn", "year", "genre", "pages"))
failure(expect_named(books, c("title", "author")))
#> Expected `books` to have names `c("title", "author")`.
#> Differences:
#> `actual`:   "title" "author" "isbn" "year" "genre" "pages"
#> `expected`: "title" "author"
#>
expect_named(books, rev(names(books)), ignore.order = TRUE)

# Sets: order and duplicates do not matter.
expect_setequal(genres, rev(genres))
failure(expect_setequal(genres, c("fiction", "poetry", "cooking")))
#> Expected `genres` to have the same values as `c("fiction", "poetry", "cooking")`.
#> Actual: "science fiction", "classic", "fiction", "mystery", "non-fiction", "poetry"
#> Expected: "fiction", "poetry", "cooking"
#> Needs: "science fiction", "classic", "mystery", "non-fiction"
#> Absent: "cooking"

# Named lists: the same names and values, in any order.
expect_mapequal(list(a = 1, b = 2), list(b = 2, a = 1))
failure(expect_mapequal(list(a = 1, b = 2), list(a = 1, b = 3)))
#> Expected `list(a = 1, b = 2)` to contain the same values as `list(a = 1, b = 3)`.
#> Differences:
#>   `actual$b`: 2.0
#> `expected$b`: 3.0
#>

# Membership: expect_contains() and expect_in() are the two directions.
expect_contains(genres, c("poetry", "classic"))
expect_in(c("poetry", "classic"), genres)
failure(expect_contains(genres, "cooking"))
#> Expected `genres` to contain all values in "cooking".
#> Actual: "science fiction", "classic", "fiction", "mystery", "non-fiction", "poetry"
#> Expected: "cooking"
#> Missing: "cooking"
failure(expect_in("cooking", genres))
#> Expected "cooking" to only contain values from `genres`.
#> Actual: "cooking"
#> Expected: "science fiction", "classic", "fiction", "mystery", "non-fiction", "poetry"
#> Invalid: "cooking"

# Numeric comparisons and text matches.
long <- books[books$pages > 400 & !is.na(books$pages), ]
expect_lt(nrow(long), 5L)
expect_gt(mean(books$year, na.rm = TRUE), 1900)
failure(expect_gt(nrow(books), 16L))
#> Expected `nrow(books)` > 16L.
#> Actual comparison: 16 <= 16
#> Difference: 0 <= 0
expect_gte(nrow(books), 16L)
expect_match(books$title[[1L]], "^The ")
failure(expect_match(books$title[[1L]], "^A "))
#> Expected `books$title[[1L]]` to match regexp "^A ".
#> Actual text:
#> ✖ │ The Dispossessed
expect_no_match(books$title[[1L]], "cooking")

# Every element at once, with a better message than expect_true(all(...)).
expect_all_true(nchar(books$title) > 0L)
failure(expect_all_true(!is.na(books$pages)))
#> Expected every element of `!is.na(books$pages)` to equal TRUE.
#> Differences:
#> `actual[3:9]`:   TRUE TRUE TRUE FALSE TRUE TRUE TRUE
#> `expected[3:9]`: TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE  TRUE TRUE TRUE
#>
#> `actual[12:16]`:   TRUE TRUE TRUE FALSE TRUE
#> `expected[12:16]`: TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE  TRUE
#>
failure(expect_true(all(!is.na(books$pages))))
#> Expected `all(!is.na(books$pages))` to be TRUE.
#> Differences:
#> `actual`:   FALSE
#> `expected`: TRUE
#>

Source: testthat package documentation: expect_setequal, expect_contains and expect_in

The last two calls show why expect_all_true() exists: for the same vector it prints the two stretches of the vector (actual[3:9] and actual[12:16]) around the two FALSE elements, so the missing page counts can be found, and expect_true(all(...)) can only say that actual is FALSE. A few of these are easy to mix up. expect_setequal() is about elements and ignores order; expect_equal() of two vectors does not. expect_contains(genres, "poetry") has the larger set first and expect_in("poetry", genres) the smaller, so the two read in opposite orders. For a named list, expect_mapequal() compares the content and not the order of the names.

Conditions: errors, warnings and messages

expect_error(), expect_warning(), expect_message() and the general expect_condition() check that the code signals the condition. The arguments are a regular expression for the message (regexp), a condition class (class), fixed = TRUE to match the text literally, and inherit to match across the parent errors of chained errors. They return the captured condition, so it can be examined, and they are the tools to test the paths that a function rejects (see Defensive Programming and Input Validation and Conditions and Error Handling).

In the third edition each of them captures at most one condition, the first one that matches the regexp and class, and lets every other condition bubble up. A condition that does not match is therefore not reported as "the message differs" but as the raw error, warning or message that it is; in a test, an unmatched error becomes an error of the test. The message is a regular expression, which is the usual cause of surprises with parentheses and dots (fixed = TRUE turns that off), and matching a message makes a test as fragile as the message. Prefer class = where the condition has one. If what you want to check is that the message is readable, use expect_snapshot(), which shows it in full.

library(testthat)
Sys.setenv(TESTTHAT_EDITION = "3")
source("scenario.R")

failure <- \(code) tryCatch(code, error = \(e) cat(conditionMessage(e), "\n"))

# expect_error() takes a regular expression for the message...
expect_error(book(""), "a book needs a title")
# ...fixed = TRUE when the message holds regular-expression characters...
expect_error(
  new_book(title = 1), "is.character(title) is not TRUE", fixed = TRUE
)
# ...and a class, which is much less fragile than the text.
expect_error(stop("no such shelf"), class = "simpleError")

# A message that does not match.
failure(expect_error(book(""), "a book needs an author"))
#> a book needs a title

# Code that does not fail, or fails in a different way.
failure(expect_error(book("A title")))
#> Expected `book("A title")` to throw a error.
failure(expect_error(stop("something else"), "a book needs a title"))
#> something else

# Warnings and messages.
expect_warning(as.integer("x"), "NAs introduced by coercion")
expect_message(message("loading"), "loading")
failure(expect_warning(1 + 1))
#> Expected `1 + 1` to throw a warning.

# A custom condition class is matched by class =.
shelf_condition <- structure(
  class = c("shelf_overdue", "warning", "condition"),
  list(message = "3 loans are overdue", call = NULL)
)
expect_warning(warning(shelf_condition), class = "shelf_overdue")
expect_condition(warning(shelf_condition), "overdue")

# The expectation returns the condition, so you can inspect it.
cnd <- expect_error(book(""), "title")
class(cnd)
#> [1] "simpleError" "error"       "condition"
conditionMessage(cnd)
#> [1] "a book needs a title"

# No condition at all.
expect_no_error(book("A title"))
expect_no_warning(as.integer("1"))
expect_no_message(1 + 1)
failure(expect_no_error(book("")))
#> Expected `book("")` not to throw any errors.
#> Actually got a <simpleError> with message:
#>   a book needs a title
failure(expect_no_warning(as.integer("x")))
#> Expected `as.integer("x")` not to throw any warnings.
#> Actually got a <simpleWarning> with message:
#>   NAs introduced by coercion

Source: testthat package documentation: expect_error, expect_warning and expect_message

Read the three failing examples carefully. In the first, expect_error(book(""), "a book needs an author"), the error that the code really signals does not match the pattern, so it escapes the expectation: the helper prints the message of the real error, a book needs a title, and not a report that the pattern differed. The second, expect_error(book("A title")), reports Expected ... to throw a error. because the code returns normally (the article "a" before "error" is the real testthat text). In the third, the error something else escapes in the same way. The value returned by expect_error() is the condition (class(cnd) is "simpleError" "error" "condition"), so conditionMessage(cnd) is available. The last group is expect_no_error(), expect_no_warning(), expect_no_message() and expect_no_condition(), which assert that the code runs without that condition and print the condition when it does not.

The expect_no_*() expectations (experimental when added in testthat 3.1.5, stable since 3.2.0) are the replacements for expect_error(code, NA). Two cautions apply to them. Writing R Extensions tells package authors not to test for the absence of warnings, because later versions of R or of other packages may add warnings (some deprecation notices are meant to stay for a long time) and the tests should not turn them into failures; and it advises against testing the exact text of messages produced by R or by other packages, which can change and be translated. Both are good reasons to expect_no_warning() only about code that you own, and to test messages of your own functions, not R’s.

Source: Writing R Extensions: Writing portable packages

Output, silence and visibility

expect_output(code, regexp) checks what the code prints to the standard output. regexp = NA asserts that nothing is printed. expect_silent() asserts that the code prints nothing, signals no message and no warning; expect_visible() and expect_invisible() check whether the value of the call is printed at the console. Printing is done by print() methods and by cat(), so these are the tools for testing a print method such as print.book(), with the caveat that a test of the exact layout of a print method is more convenient as a snapshot.

library(testthat)
Sys.setenv(TESTTHAT_EDITION = "3")
source("scenario.R")

failure <- \(code) tryCatch(code, error = \(e) cat(conditionMessage(e), "\n"))

b <- book("Paper Moons", "Noor Haddad")

# Printed output: a regular expression, or NA for "no output at all".
expect_output(print(b), "n.d.")
failure(expect_output(print(b), "2018"))
#> Expected output from `print(b)` to match regexp "2018".
#> Actual output:
#> ✖ │ <book> Paper Moons (Noor Haddad, n.d.)
expect_output(invisible(b), NA)
failure(expect_output(print(b), NA))
#> Expected `print(b)` to produce no output.
#> Actual output:
#> <book> Paper Moons (Noor Haddad, n.d.)

# capture.output() gives the text that expect_output() matches against.
out <- capture.output(print(b))
out
#> [1] "<book> Paper Moons (Noor Haddad, n.d.) "
expect_identical(out, "<book> Paper Moons (Noor Haddad, n.d.) ")

# expect_silent(): no output, no messages, no warnings.
expect_silent(format(b))
failure(expect_silent(print(b)))
#> Expected `print(b)` to run silently.
#> Actual noise: output.
failure(expect_silent(as.integer("x")))
#> Expected `as.integer("x")` to run silently.
#> Actual noise: warnings.

# Visible and invisible results.
expect_invisible(invisible(1))
expect_visible(format(b))
failure(expect_invisible(format(b)))
#> Expected `format(b)` to return invisibly.
#> Actual visibility: visible.

Source: testthat package documentation: expect_output and expect_silent

Your own expectations: pass(), fail() and succeed()

An expectation that a package needs several times can be written as a function. It has four parts: capture the value and its label with quasi_label(rlang::enquo(object)), call fail(message) for each way the value can violate the expectation, call pass() when it does not, and return the input invisibly so that the expectation can be piped. The message has the same shape as the built-in ones: the first element says what was expected, the following ones what was seen. testthat 3.3.0 added pass(), for use in place of succeed(), which still works and just records a success with a message. Put such functions in a helper-*.R file, so that every test file has them.

Because an expectation is a function it can have bugs, and it must signal exactly one success or exactly one failure. expect_success() and expect_failure() check that, and expect_snapshot_failure() records the failure message of an expectation in a snapshot. The script uses the built package through shelf:: calls and installs the stop reporter without praise.

library(testthat)
Sys.setenv(TESTTHAT_EDITION = "3")
set_reporter(StopReporter$new(praise = FALSE))
books <- shelf::books

# A custom expectation: capture the label, fail or pass, return the input.
expect_valid_isbn <- function(object) {
  act <- quasi_label(rlang::enquo(object))
  ok <- shelf::is_valid_isbn13(act$val)
  if (!all(ok)) {
    fail(c(
      sprintf("Expected every element of %s to be a valid ISBN-13.", act$lab),
      sprintf("Invalid: %s", toString(dQuote(act$val[!ok], FALSE)))
    ))
  } else {
    pass()
  }
  invisible(act$val)
}

# Expectations are functions: test them with expect_success()/expect_failure().
test_that("expect_valid_isbn() reports one success or one failure", {
  expect_success(expect_valid_isbn(books$isbn[1:5]))
  expect_failure(expect_valid_isbn(books$isbn))
})

# And look at the message that a user would see.
tryCatch(
  test_that("the failure message names the bad ISBNs", {
    expect_valid_isbn(books$isbn)
  }),
  error = \(e) invisible(NULL)
)
#> ── Failure: the failure message names the bad ISBNs ────────────────────────────
#> Expected every element of `books$isbn` to be a valid ISBN-13.
#> Invalid: "", "978-0-01-100112-9"

Source: testthat package documentation: Custom expectations

The families, summarised:

Question Expectation Note

Same value?

expect_identical(), expect_equal()

waldo diffs in the third edition; tolerance, ignore_attr

TRUE, FALSE, NULL?

expect_true(), expect_false(), expect_null()

a length-1 logical, not "truthy"

Which type or class?

expect_type(), expect_s3_class(), expect_s4_class(), expect_s7_class(), expect_r6_class(), expect_vector(), expect_shape()

replace expect_is()

How long, which names?

expect_length(), expect_named()

Which elements?

expect_setequal(), expect_mapequal(), expect_contains(), expect_in(), expect_disjoint(), expect_all_equal(), expect_all_true(), expect_all_false()

sets ignore order

Bigger or smaller?

expect_lt(), expect_lte(), expect_gt(), expect_gte()

numbers, dates, times

Text?

expect_match(), expect_no_match()

regular expressions

A condition?

expect_error(), expect_warning(), expect_message(), expect_condition(), and the expect_no_*() forms

one captured condition; class =

Printed output?

expect_output(), expect_silent(), expect_visible(), expect_invisible()

A recorded result?

expect_snapshot(), expect_snapshot_value(), expect_snapshot_file(), expect_snapshot_error(), expect_snapshot_warning()

see Snapshot tests

Something else?

fail(), pass(), succeed(), skip()

custom expectations and skips

Source: testthat package documentation: Reference index

Reading a failure

A test suite earns its keep when something breaks, so it is worth looking at what a break looks like. The experiment below adds a scratch test file to a copy of the package with one problem of each kind: a number that is off by one, a string that differs in case, an expect_error() whose regular expression does not match the real message, an error raised by the code under test, and a warning raised while an expectation evaluates its argument. The file is tests/testthat/test-failing.R, written by a script and deleted again at the end:

# A scratch test file with one problem of each kind (removed again at the end).
writeLines(
  trimws(r"---(
test_that("overdue_loans() finds 31 late loans", {
  out <- overdue_loans(loans, today = shelf_fixed_today)
  expect_equal(nrow(out), 31L)
})

test_that("book() lower-cases the title", {
  expect_identical(book("Salt and Static")$title, "salt and static")
})

test_that("a bad ISBN is rejected", {
  expect_error(book("X", isbn = "9780001000101"), "invalid isbn")
})

test_that("clean_books() accepts a partial catalogue", {
  cleaned <- clean_books(books[, c("title", "author")])
  expect_identical(nrow(cleaned), 16L)
})

test_that("a plain coercion warns", {
  expect_identical(as.integer("x"), NA_integer_)
})
)---", whitespace = "\n"),
  "tests/testthat/test-failing.R"
)

devtools::test(filter = "failing")

unlink("tests/testthat/test-failing.R")

Source: testthat package documentation: Special files

The script writes the file with writeLines() (the long string in the middle of the script is the content of test-failing.R), then runs only that file with devtools::test(filter = "failing"), and deletes the file. The filter is a regular expression matched against the part of the file name between test- and .R. The output is the real report of testthat 3.3.2, from the start of the run to the end of the failures; the spinner lines that a terminal overwrites, the second copy of the failures that the reporter prints under the Failed tests heading, and the random word of encouragement that closes a failing run are left out:

shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days
✔ | F W  S  OK | Context

✖ | 4 1      1 | failing
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

`expected`: 31


Failure ('test-failing.R:7:3'): book() lower-cases the title
Expected `book("Salt and Static")$title` to be identical to "salt and static".
Differences:
`actual`:   "Salt and Static"
`expected`: "salt and static"


Error ('test-failing.R:11:3'): a bad ISBN is rejected

 2. │ └─testthat:::expect_condition_matching_(...)
 3. │   └─testthat:::quasi_capture(...)
 4. │     ├─testthat (local) .capture(...)

 6. │     └─rlang::eval_bare(quo_get_expr(.quo), quo_get_env(.quo))
 7. └─shelf::book("X", isbn = "9780001000101")

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

══ Results ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
[ FAIL 4 | WARN 1 | SKIP 0 | PASS 1 ]

Source: devtools package documentation: test

The line that starts with a cross, ✖ | 4 1 1 | failing, is the progress line of the file: the columns are the failures (F), warnings (W), skips (S) and passes (OK) so far, which is why the empty column is the skips. Each problem then gets a block that starts with its kind and its place, Failure ('test-failing.R:3:3'), which is the file, the line and the column of the expectation (a clickable link in a terminal that supports hyperlinks), followed by the description of the test.

  • The first failure is expect_equal(nrow(out), 31L): testthat names the expression it evaluated, nrow(out), shows both values under actual and expected and does not say anything else, because there is nothing else to say about two numbers. The difference to a hand-written expect_true(nrow(out) == 31L), whose report would be nrow(out) == 31L is not TRUE, is the point of the dedicated expectations.

  • The second is the same for strings; the waldo display lines the strings up under each other.

  • The third is the pitfall of the previous section. The pattern "invalid isbn" is case-sensitive and the real message is invalid ISBN-13: 9780001000101, so the expectation does not match; in the third edition the real error is not swallowed but escapes, and the test is reported as an Error, with the message of the error under the heading and a backtrace of the calls. The backtrace shows where the error was raised (shelf::validate_book()) and, because devtools loads the package from source with source references, the file and line (shelf/R/book.R:28:3, relative to the directory that holds the package; paths shortened).

  • The fourth is a bug that the test found in the code: calling clean_books() with only two columns fails with replacement has 0 rows, data has 16, which is a symptom and not a diagnosis: the function assigns tolower(squish(books$genre)) to books$genre, and for a catalogue without a genre column that value has length zero. The report prints the call stack with the source location of the assignment in shelf/R/clean.R:23:3. A caller deserves a message that names the missing column (see Defensive Programming and Input Validation).

  • The last block is a warning, NAs introduced by coercion, which comes from evaluating as.integer("x") as the argument of the expectation. The expectation itself passed (PASS 1); warnings are counted separately and reported, and a package whose tests warn is a package whose check logs are noisy. Wrap the call in suppressWarnings() or test the warning with expect_warning().

The totals at the end, [ FAIL 4 | WARN 1 | SKIP 0 | PASS 1 ], are the line that every reporter finishes with, and devtools::test() returns normally even when tests fail (its argument stop_on_failure defaults to FALSE), unlike test_check(), which signals an error.

The same failure in R CMD check

Under R CMD check a failing test produces the report that a maintainer sees in the check log. To see it, one failing test file was added to a copy of the package, with the unchanged suite beside it. This is the whole file tests/testthat/test-failing.R; its expectation is false because the packaged loans contain 32 overdue loans for the fixed date, not 31:

test_that("a failing check", {
  expect_equal(nrow(overdue_loans(loans, today = shelf_fixed_today)), 31L)
})

Source: testthat package documentation: expect_equal

The package was then built and checked with the commands of the section on R CMD check (R CMD build shelf, then R CMD check --as-cran --no-manual on the tarball). The platform header of the log and the checks that are not about tests are trimmed from the excerpt. The check log shows the last 13 lines of the test output, which is the default of the environment variable _R_CHECK_TESTS_NLINES_, and says where the whole output went: a file testthat.Rout.fail in the check directory.

  Running ‘testthat.R’

Running the tests in ‘tests/testthat.R’ failed.
Last 13 lines of output:
  ══ Skipped tests (2) ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  • On CRAN (2): 'test-book.R:39:1', 'test-loans.R:40:3'

  ══ Failed tests ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  ── Failure ('test-failing.R:2:3'): a failing check ─────────────────────────────
  Expected `nrow(overdue_loans(loans, today = shelf_fixed_today))` to equal 31L.
  Differences:
    `actual`: 32
  `expected`: 31


  [ FAIL 1 | WARN 0 | SKIP 2 | PASS 49 ]
  Error:

Source: R Internals: Tools

The two skips on CRAN in the excerpt are explained in Skipping tests, and Error: ! Test failures. followed by Execution halted is how test_check() ends a failing run: the check reports the test run as ERROR, and the status of the whole check is 1 ERROR. Since testthat 3.3.0, a test run under R CMD check also writes a reprex for each failing expectation into tests/testthat/_problems/ of the check directory, so that the failure can be reproduced without a copy of the whole package. (The line Saving _problems/test-failing-2.R in the full output is that happening; the 2 is the line of the failing expectation.) After the failing check, the files of the test directory of the check and the reprex file were:

shelf.Rcheck/tests:
startup.Rs
testthat
testthat.R
testthat.Rout.fail

shelf.Rcheck/tests/testthat/_problems:
test-failing-2.R

Source: testthat package documentation: extract_test

# Extracted from test-failing.R:2

# setup ------------------------------------------------------------------------
library(testthat)
test_env <- simulate_test_env(package = "shelf", path = "..")
attach(test_env, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

# test -------------------------------------------------------------------------
expect_equal(nrow(overdue_loans(loans, today = shelf_fixed_today)), 31L)

Source: testthat package documentation: extract_test

simulate_test_env() builds the environment that a test would run in, with the package namespace as parent and the helper files loaded, and attach(test_env, ...) makes it the search path, so that the one expectation can be run from a plain R session. Setting the environment variable TESTTHAT_PROBLEMS=false turns the files off.

To investigate a failure in your own session, the usual route is not the reprex but devtools::load_all() followed by running the test body line by line: the helper file is attached by load_all(), and everything in the package, internal functions included, is visible. The commands of Debugging (browser(), traceback(), options(error = recover)) work inside a test as they do anywhere. testthat::local_test_context() reproduces the options and environment variables that a test sets before running, when the failure depends on them.

Describing behaviour with describe() and it()

describe() and it() are a second way of writing the same tests, in the style of behaviour-driven development tools such as RSpec for Ruby and Mocha for JavaScript. A describe() block names a component, an it() inside it names one specification, and the pair reads as a sentence: "is_valid_isbn13() accepts hyphenated and bare forms of a valid ISBN". The interface has been in testthat since version 0.9 (2014), and it() was exported in 3.1.8 so that it can be run interactively. Each it() is evaluated in its own environment like a test_that() block, describe() blocks can be nested, and a specification without code, it("handles NA"), is reported as a skipped test with the reason empty test, which makes it a to-do list that the suite shows. The help page says to use describe() to verify that you implement the right things and test_that() to ensure you do the things right: in practice most packages use test_that() and keep describe() for functions with several specifications.

The shelf suite has one describe() block, in test-book.R:

describe("is_valid_isbn13()", {
  it("accepts hyphenated and bare forms of a valid ISBN", {
    expect_identical(
      is_valid_isbn13(c("978-0-00-100010-0", "9780001000100")),
      c(TRUE, TRUE)
    )
  })
  it("rejects wrong check digits, short strings, empty strings and NA", {
    expect_identical(
      is_valid_isbn13(c("9780001000101", "978030640615", "", NA)),
      c(FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE)
    )
  })
  it("returns a logical of the same length, including length zero", {
    expect_identical(is_valid_isbn13(character()), logical())
  })
})

Source: testthat package documentation: describe

The names of the three tests in a report or in the data frame that the runner returns are the descriptions joined with /: is_valid_isbn13() / accepts hyphenated and bare forms of a valid ISBN. test_file() can run one test of a file with its desc argument (testthat 3.2.0), and since testthat 3.3.0 desc can be a character vector that names the path through nested blocks, so one it() of a describe() is selected by the two descriptions. The first row of the result is the specification that ran, and the second the enclosing describe(), which contains no expectation of its own:

library(testthat)

# Run one specification of the describe() block of test-book.R by its path.
res <- test_file(
  "tests/testthat/test-book.R",
  desc = c(
    "is_valid_isbn13()",
    "rejects wrong check digits, short strings, empty strings and NA"
  ),
  package = "shelf", load_package = "source", reporter = "silent"
)
results <- as.data.frame(res)
results$test
results$nb
#> shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days
#> [1] "is_valid_isbn13() / rejects wrong check digits, short strings, empty strings and NA"
#> [2] "is_valid_isbn13()"
#> [1] 1 0

Source: testthat package documentation: test_file

Snapshot tests

Some expected results are awkward to write as code: output with many quotes and line breaks, output too long to put in a test file, a print method or an error message whose point is that a human finds it readable. For these testthat has snapshot tests, also called golden tests: instead of describing the expected result in code, the expectation runs the code, records what happened in a separate Markdown file under tests/testthat/_snaps/, and on later runs compares the new result with the recorded one. They were added in testthat 3.0.0 and expect_snapshot() stopped being experimental in 3.1.0. Snapshots work only in the third edition (in the second, expect_snapshot() stops with an error saying that expect_snapshot() requires the 3rd edition, as the section on common errors shows) and are stored only when a whole test file runs, with test_file(), test_dir() or one of the functions built on them; run at the console, a snapshot expectation only displays the result, and the testthat article shows it saying that it can’t save or compare to a reference when testing interactively.

The first run: recording

expect_snapshot(code) runs code as if typed at the console and records the code, the printed output, the messages, the warnings and the errors. The first time it runs there is nothing to compare with, so testthat records the result and reports it as a warning, so that you read it before you commit it. The experiment below deletes the _snaps directory of the copy of the package and runs the tests twice. The spinner lines of devtools::test() are left out:

# Throw the stored snapshots away to see what a first run looks like.
unlink("tests/testthat/_snaps", recursive = TRUE)
devtools::test()
list.files("tests/testthat/_snaps")
devtools::test()

Source: testthat package documentation: Snapshot tests

ℹ Testing shelf
shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days

Source: testthat package documentation: Snapshot tests

In the first run the two warnings, WARN 2, are Adding new snapshot: followed by the code and the output that were recorded, and the file is back: list.files() shows book.md. In the second run the same two expectations pass without any report and the totals are the ones of the normal run. The recorded file is the _snaps/book.md shown earlier. Its format is a subset of Markdown on purpose, so that a reviewer can read changes in a pull request without running anything. Each test is a level-one heading; each snapshot is indented by four spaces as a code block; snapshots of the same test are separated by ---; inside one, the labels Code, Output, Message and Condition say what the lines below are. The file is named after the test file, test-book.R giving _snaps/book.md. A test that is deleted loses its snapshot the next time the whole suite runs, and a snapshot file with no snapshots left is deleted.

On a continuous integration server a new snapshot is a failure and not a warning (see Snapshots on CI). A snapshot is part of the code and goes in version control; reviewing the diff of _snaps/ is the review of the behaviour change.

When a snapshot changes

If the output changes, the expectation fails, shows a diff of the old and the new, and writes the new result to book.new.md next to the recorded file. The experiment below changes print.book() so that it prints <Book> instead of <book>, runs the tests of that file, accepts the change with snapshot_accept(), shows what changed in book.md, and restores the source and the snapshot:

# Remember the originals so that the script can put them back at the end.
book_r <- readLines("R/book.R")
snap <- readLines("tests/testthat/_snaps/book.md")

# Change what print.book() prints: "<book>" becomes "<Book>".
changed <- sub('cat("<book>"', 'cat("<Book>"', book_r, fixed = TRUE)
writeLines(changed, "R/book.R")

# The snapshot no longer matches: the test fails and a .new.md file appears.
devtools::test(filter = "book")
list.files("tests/testthat/_snaps")

# The change is deliberate: accept it, which replaces book.md by book.new.md.
testthat::snapshot_accept("book")
list.files("tests/testthat/_snaps")
setdiff(readLines("tests/testthat/_snaps/book.md"), snap)

# Clean up: restore the source and the snapshot.
writeLines(book_r, "R/book.R")
writeLines(snap, "tests/testthat/_snaps/book.md")

Source: testthat package documentation: snapshot_accept

Source: testthat package documentation: snapshot_accept

The report is a diff in which - lines are the recorded result and + lines the new one, with the lines Code and print(b) as context, and the two lines at the end of the report name the remedies. snapshot_accept("book") replaces book.md by book.new.md, which is the right step only when the change is the one intended; if it is not, fix the code and the test passes again, and the .new.md file goes away. snapshot_review("book") opens a Shiny application (it needs the shiny package) that shows each pending change and lets you accept or reject it; snapshot_reject() deletes the .new.md files (testthat 3.3.0). The recorded change is a single line, as setdiff() of the two versions of book.md shows, with the leading spaces of the code-block indentation.

Snapshots on CI

A snapshot that has no stored version is only a warning on a developer’s machine, so that the first run records it. On a continuous-integration server it is a failure, because a missing snapshot there almost always means that the snapshot file was never committed (testthat 3.3.0). The server is recognised by the environment variable CI, which hosted services set to true. The experiment sets it by hand, after remembering the stored snapshot and deleting it, runs the tests of test-book.R, and puts the snapshot back:

# Remember the stored snapshot, then throw it away to simulate a forgotten file.
snap <- readLines("tests/testthat/_snaps/book.md")
unlink("tests/testthat/_snaps", recursive = TRUE)

# CI services set CI=true (GitHub Actions does): a new snapshot now fails.
Sys.setenv(CI = "true")
devtools::test(filter = "book")

# Put the stored snapshot back.
dir.create("tests/testthat/_snaps", showWarnings = FALSE)
writeLines(snap, "tests/testthat/_snaps/book.md")

Source: testthat package documentation: Snapshot tests

Source: testthat package documentation: expect_snapshot

The two blocks are the same as the two warnings of the first run, but they are reported as Failure and the totals are [ FAIL 2 | WARN 0 | SKIP 0 | PASS 24 ] (PASS 24 counts the passes in test-book.R alone, since the filter selected that file). The content that was going to be recorded is shown, which is what you need to compare with the file you meant to commit. The remedy is to run the tests locally, read the snapshot, and commit tests/testthat/_snaps/. On a machine where the stored file exists but some of its snapshots differ the report is the diff of the previous section, whatever the value of CI. (The random line of encouragement that the progress reporter prints after a failing run is left out of the transcript.)

Other snapshot expectations

The six tests below, again in a scratch file of the copy of the package, show the other forms. They run once with the reporter silenced, and the script prints the files that the first run created:

# A scratch test file that uses the other snapshot expectations.
writeLines(
  trimws(r"---(
test_that("an invalid book is snapshotted with its error", {
  expect_snapshot(book("X", isbn = "9780001000101"), error = TRUE)
})

test_that("messages and warnings are recorded with the code", {
  expect_snapshot({
    x <- as.integer("x")
    message("loaded ", nrow(books), " books")
    summary(book("Paper Moons", "Noor Haddad", pages = 120))
  })
})

test_that("a value is snapshotted in a readable form", {
  expect_snapshot_value(loans_per_month(loans)[1:2, ], style = "deparse")
})

test_that("a file is snapshotted as a whole", {
  path <- withr::local_tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
  write.csv(loans_per_month(loans)[1:3, ], path, row.names = FALSE)
  expect_snapshot_file(path, "months.csv")
})

test_that("variable text is cleaned with transform", {
  path <- withr::local_tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
  expect_snapshot(
    cat("saved to", path, "\n"),
    transform = \(lines) gsub(path, "<path>", lines, fixed = TRUE)
  )
})

test_that("a snapshot can depend on the R version", {
  variant <- paste0("r", getRversion()$major, ".", getRversion()$minor)
  expect_snapshot(print(loans_per_month(loans)[1:2, ]), variant = variant)
})
)---", whitespace = "\n"),
  "tests/testthat/test-snapshots.R"
)

# The first run creates every snapshot (the reporter is silenced here).
invisible(devtools::test(filter = "snapshots", reporter = "silent"))
list.files("tests/testthat/_snaps", recursive = TRUE)
cat(readLines("tests/testthat/_snaps/snapshots.md"), sep = "\n")
cat(readLines("tests/testthat/_snaps/snapshots/months.csv"), sep = "\n")
cat(readLines("tests/testthat/_snaps/r4.6/snapshots.md"), sep = "\n")

# Clean up the scratch test and its snapshots.
unlink("tests/testthat/test-snapshots.R")
unlink(
  file.path("tests/testthat/_snaps", c("snapshots.md", "snapshots", "r4.6")),
  recursive = TRUE
)
list.files("tests/testthat/_snaps")
