Source: testthat package documentation: expect_snapshot_file

  • error = TRUE is required to record an error. expect_snapshot(book("X", isbn = "9780001000101")) without it fails, because an unexpected error is a failure (even on CRAN); with it, the error is recorded as a Condition and the test passes, and an expected error that does not occur is a failure. The error argument checks that at least one expression in the block errors, not that every one does. The display shows the call and the message the way R prints them at the console; it does not include the class of the condition unless cnd_class = TRUE, because classes are added by upstream packages and R itself (testthat 3.1.1 introduced the argument and 3.2.0 made the class-free display the default for every package).

  • One expect_snapshot() can hold several statements, as the second test does: the assignment with a warning, a message, and a call whose printed value is recorded. Each statement is recorded under its own Code heading, followed by Output, Message or Condition for what it produced.

  • expect_snapshot_value(x, style) records the value instead of the printed text. The styles are "json" (the default; the simplest output, for simple objects, written with the jsonlite package), "json2" (more verbose, for a wider range of objects), "deparse" (a depiction of the object as R code) and "serialize" (a binary serialization that works for nearly any object and is opaque); tolerance makes the comparison numerical, like expect_equal(). In the example, deparse records two lines of R code that rebuild the data frame.

  • expect_snapshot_file(path, name) snapshots a whole file, such as a plot or a written CSV, in _snaps/<test file>/<name>, one file for each expectation. A changed file cannot be diffed automatically: the new version is saved as months.new.csv and snapshot_review() shows both. The function is usually called through a wrapper that skips the test on platforms where the output is not reproducible, and a wrapper should call announce_snapshot_file() so that testthat does not delete a snapshot that was not regenerated because the test was skipped. For plots testthat points to the vdiffr package, which is not installed here and is named only.

  • transform = \(lines) ... rewrites the lines before they are recorded, which is how to remove temporary paths, versions, times and other things that vary. Here the temporary path from withr::local_tempfile() is replaced by <path>; without the transform, the snapshot would change on every run, and the test would fail on every run after the first.

  • variant = "r4.6" stores the result in _snaps/r4.6/snapshots.md instead of _snaps/snapshots.md, so that one test can record the output that differs by operating system, R version or dependency version, each in its own file. testthat calls variants an advanced feature: once they exist, you are responsible for deleting the ones that are no longer used, and for having a way to get changed snapshots out of the CI system and back into the repository.

Snapshots and CRAN

expect_snapshot() has the argument cran = FALSE: by default the snapshot expectations are not verified on CRAN, because snapshot tests rely on details of the output that dependencies may change (the help page gives that reason). On CRAN they return without recording or comparing anything. In testthat 3.3.0 they stopped skipping the rest of the test (as skip_on_cran() would) and began returning right away, neither passing nor failing, and the test that contains them is reported as skipped on CRAN. That is what the real R CMD check --as-cran of the package shows: SKIP 2, the snapshot test in test-book.R and the skip_on_cran() test in test-loans.R, and PASS 49 instead of the PASS 52 of devtools::test() (see Skipping tests). Do not set cran = TRUE for text that depends on other packages or on R’s own messages. Writing R Extensions warns against exactly that: R’s messages change between versions and are translated.

When to use a snapshot

A snapshot is a record of what the code did, which is not the same as a statement of what it should do. A reviewer who accepts a changed snapshot without reading it has turned the test off. Use a snapshot where a human is the judge (a print method, a cli message, the wording of an error), where the output is long and only its stability matters, or as a first test of legacy code. Use expect_equal() and its relatives for values and structure, which a snapshot hides in text, and expect_error(class = ) where an error has a class; in the shelf suite, describe() and expect_identical() test the logic, and only the two print methods are snapshots. Keep the code in a snapshot small, so that a failure diff points at one thing.

Fixtures and withr

A test should leave the world as it found it. The state after test number i is the starting state of test i + 1, so a test that sets an option, an environment variable or the working directory and forgets to undo it makes the next test depend on it, and the failures that result appear in a different place from the cause. The test-fixtures article of testthat lists the things a test typically changes: a file or a directory, a resource on an external system, an R option, an environment variable, the working directory, or the state of the package under test. A fixture in this sense is a piece of code that sets one of them up for the length of a test and removes it afterwards.

testthat does not contain the tools for this itself; it relies on the package withr (3.0.3 here, an add-on package, listed under Suggests in shelf because the tests call it with ::). Its functions come in pairs: with_*() changes something for the evaluation of one expression and local_*() changes it until the surrounding function, or the surrounding test_that() block, ends. The five that cover most tests are:

Change withr function

Create a temporary file that is deleted afterwards

withr::local_tempfile()

Create a temporary directory

withr::local_tempdir()

Set an R option

withr::local_options()

Set an environment variable

withr::local_envvar()

Change the working directory

withr::local_dir()

Source: testthat package documentation: Test fixtures

withr has many more: local_seed() and with_seed() for the random-number generator, local_timezone(), local_locale(), local_language() and local_collate() for the things that differ between machines, local_path(), local_libpaths(), local_connection(), local_db_connection(), local_package() and the graphics devices (local_png(), local_pdf(), local_svg()). The script below uses the most common ones inside tests and prints, after each test, that the state is back. It sets the stop reporter without praise so that a passing test prints nothing.

library(testthat)
Sys.setenv(TESTTHAT_EDITION = "3")
set_reporter(StopReporter$new(praise = FALSE))
source("scenario.R")

# A temporary file that is deleted when the test ends.
test_that("local_tempfile() cleans up after the test", {
  path <- withr::local_tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
  write.csv(head(books, 3L), path, row.names = FALSE)
  expect_true(file.exists(path))
  expect_identical(nrow(read.csv(path)), 3L)
  assign("kept_path", path, envir = globalenv())
})
file.exists(kept_path)
#> [1] FALSE

# An option, an environment variable and the working directory.
test_that("options, environment variables and directories are restored", {
  withr::local_options(digits = 3L, shelf.loan_days = 14L)
  withr::local_envvar(SHELF_ENV = "test")
  dir <- withr::local_tempdir()
  withr::local_dir(dir)
  expect_identical(Sys.getenv("SHELF_ENV"), "test")
  expect_identical(getOption("shelf.loan_days"), 14L)
  expect_identical(format(pi), "3.14")
  expect_identical(list.files(), character())
})
c(Sys.getenv("SHELF_ENV", "<unset>"), format(pi), basename(getwd()))
#> [1] "<unset>"  "3.141593" "shelf"
is.null(getOption("shelf.loan_days"))
#> [1] TRUE

# A seed that does not disturb the caller's random number stream.
set.seed(1)
before <- runif(1)
set.seed(1)
test_that("with_seed() makes a random sample reproducible", {
  s1 <- withr::with_seed(42, sample(nrow(books), 3L))
  s2 <- withr::with_seed(42, sample(nrow(books), 3L))
  expect_identical(s1, s2)
})
identical(runif(1), before)
#> [1] TRUE

# defer() runs a cleanup when the test finishes, last in, first out.
test_that("defer() registers cleanups that run in reverse order", {
  withr::defer(cat("cleanup 1\n"))
  withr::defer(cat("cleanup 2\n"))
  cat("test body\n")
  expect_true(TRUE)
})
#> test body
#> cleanup 2
#> cleanup 1

# A helper that sets the option for its caller: pass .local_envir through.
local_loan_days <- function(days, env = parent.frame()) {
  withr::local_options(shelf.loan_days = days, .local_envir = env)
  invisible(days)
}
test_that("a local_ helper changes state for one test only", {
  local_loan_days(7L)
  expect_identical(getOption("shelf.loan_days"), 7L)
})
getOption("shelf.loan_days", "<unset>")
#> [1] "<unset>"

Source: withr package documentation: Reference index

Read the output from the top.

  • The first test writes three rows of books to a temporary file and reads them back. The path is saved in a variable of the global environment only to look at it afterwards: file.exists(kept_path) is FALSE, because local_tempfile() registered the deletion of the file for the end of the test. The file lives in the session’s temporary directory, which is the only place CRAN policy allows a package to write during checks (apart from the user-specific directories of tools::R_user_dir(), which tests should not touch).

  • The second test changes an option (digits), a package option (shelf.loan_days), an environment variable and the working directory (to a temporary directory, which is itself deleted at the end). Inside the test the new values are in force (format(pi) is "3.14" with digits = 3). Outside, the line c(Sys.getenv("SHELF_ENV", "<unset>"), format(pi), basename(getwd())) shows the environment variable unset, pi printed with seven digits again, and the working directory back where it was (its last component, shelf, is the directory the script is run from); is.null(getOption("shelf.loan_days")) is TRUE because the option did not exist before.

  • The third test shows with_seed(). It runs a block with a given seed and restores the random-number stream afterwards, so runif(1) after the test continues the stream the caller had (identical(runif(1), before) is TRUE). The seed does not leak out of the test. This is the right way to test code that uses random numbers; Writing R Extensions points out that tests in a package run in a vanilla session without a seed.

  • The fourth test calls withr::defer() twice. The deferred actions run when the test ends, in the reverse order of registration: cleanup 2 is printed before cleanup 1, after the line printed by the body of the test. Last in, first out is what makes teardown correct: a file that was created inside a temporary directory must be removed before the directory.

  • The last test defines a helper, local_loan_days(), that changes an option for its caller. The helper takes an env = parent.frame() argument and passes it on as .local_envir; without that, the option would be restored when the helper itself returns, which is immediately. The final getOption("shelf.loan_days", "<unset>") prints <unset> again.

on.exit() and defer()

Base R’s on.exit() is the primitive behind all of this: it runs an expression when the current function exits, whether normally or through an error. In a test the habit is on.exit(options(old), add = TRUE, after = FALSE), where the two arguments make sure that a second on.exit() call adds to the first instead of replacing it, and that the cleanup runs in reverse order. The test-fixtures article names three drawbacks: the arguments are easy to forget, it does nothing useful at the top level of a script (the code is never run), and it cannot be put in a helper, because it is bound to the function that calls it. withr::defer() has none of them: its default behaviour is the right one, it can be told which environment to bind the cleanup to (a helper passes its caller’s environment), and at the top level of a script or the console it records the action and you run it with withr::deferred_run(). The local_*() functions are defer() applied to the most common setup actions. See Scoping, Environments and Closures for what parent.frame() is.

Source: R documentation: on.exit

The name local_ is chosen on purpose: the change is local to the function or test. The article adds that a local_ call can be scoped to a smaller part of a test with local({ ... }).

Where a fixture is applied: test, file, package

A fixture can be applied at three scopes, and the choice is a trade-off between duplication and debuggability.

  • Inside a test_that() block, which is the default. The change lasts for that test. A failing test can be reproduced in an interactive session by running the body line by line.

  • At the top of a test file, outside any test_that(). It then lasts to the end of the file, and so affects every test after it. This saves repetition, but a test that fails cannot be reproduced without first running the lines at the top. The testthat article leans towards copying the fixture into each test for exactly that reason.

  • Package-wide, in a setup file in tests/testthat/. The code of a file whose name starts with setup (by convention setup.R) runs once before any test file. Cleanup belongs in the same file, registered with withr::defer(..., teardown_env()) or withr::local_options(..., .local_envir = teardown_env()): teardown_env() is a special environment that stays alive until all the tests have run. The older approach, a teardown-*.R file, still works but is no longer recommended, because setup and cleanup in different files drift apart.

A helper file (helper-*.R) is different: it only defines things, such as the shelf_fixed_today constant and read_fixture_books() of the shelf suite, custom expectations and local_* helpers. The difference between the two matters when the tests are run interactively. Helper files are sourced by devtools::load_all() as well as by test_check() and its relatives, so the objects exist when you work on a failing test. Setup files are sourced only by the functions that run tests, not by load_all(), so after load_all() whatever a setup file would have created, such as an option, is missing. The experiment below adds a scratch setup file and a scratch test to a copy of the package, runs them, and then calls load_all() outside the tests to see which of the two is available:

# A scratch setup file and a test file that depends on it.
writeLines(
  trimws(r"---(
withr::local_options(shelf.quiet = TRUE, .local_envir = teardown_env())
message("setup-scratch.R: the setup file ran")
withr::defer(message("setup-scratch.R: the teardown ran"), teardown_env())
)---", whitespace = "\n"),
  "tests/testthat/setup-scratch.R"
)
writeLines(
  trimws(r"---(
test_that("the setup file has run before the tests", {
  expect_true(getOption("shelf.quiet"))
  expect_identical(shelf_fixed_today, as.Date("2026-06-30"))
  expect_true(file.exists(test_path("fixtures", "books-small.csv")))
  message("test-scratch.R: inside the test")
})
)---", whitespace = "\n"),
  "tests/testthat/test-scratch.R"
)

devtools::test(filter = "scratch")

# Outside a test, load_all() sources the helpers but not the setup files.
devtools::load_all(quiet = TRUE)
shelf_fixed_today
is.null(getOption("shelf.quiet"))
testthat::test_path("fixtures", "books-small.csv")

unlink(c("tests/testthat/setup-scratch.R", "tests/testthat/test-scratch.R"))

Source: testthat package documentation: Special files

[1] "tests/testthat/fixtures/books-small.csv"

Source: testthat package documentation: test_that

The setup file ran first (setup-scratch.R: the setup file ran, a message printed before the progress table), the test saw the option it set (expect_true(getOption("shelf.quiet"))) and the constant from the helper (shelf_fixed_today), found the fixture through test_path(), and the teardown message (the teardown ran) was printed after the results, when teardown_env() was cleaned up. After the run, load_all() makes shelf_fixed_today available ("2026-06-30"), but the option that the setup file set is not there (is.null(getOption("shelf.quiet")) is TRUE), and test_path() resolves the fixture relative to the tests directory. Keep setup files small for that reason: whatever they create has to be recreated by hand before a failing test can be debugged.

Data files for tests go in the tests/testthat/fixtures/ directory (any name works, since testthat ignores directories it does not know), which the shelf suite uses for books-small.csv. Reach them with test_path("fixtures", "books-small.csv"): the function returns a path that is correct whether the tests are run from the package root, from tests/testthat/ or by R CMD check. A helper that reads the file, as read_fixture_books() does, keeps the path in one place. Anything a test writes goes to withr::local_tempfile(), never into the tests directory.

Finding the test that leaks: set_state_inspector()

When a suite becomes slow to debug because some test leaves a mess, set_state_inspector() (testthat 3.1.9) registers a function that testthat calls before and after every test; it reports any difference as a warning against the test that caused it. The function returns the pieces of state to watch. The scratch file below has one polite test and two that leak, an option and an environment variable:

library(testthat)

# Ask testthat to compare these pieces of global state before and after a test.
set_state_inspector(function() {
  list(
    digits = getOption("digits"),
    shelf_env = Sys.getenv("SHELF_ENV", NA)
  )
})

writeLines(
  trimws(r"---(
test_that("a polite test restores what it changes", {
  withr::local_options(digits = 3L)
  expect_true(TRUE)
})

test_that("a test that leaks an option", {
  options(digits = 4L)
  expect_true(TRUE)
})

test_that("a test that leaks an environment variable", {
  Sys.setenv(SHELF_ENV = "leak")
  expect_true(TRUE)
})
)---", whitespace = "\n"),
  "tests/testthat/test-leaky.R"
)

devtools::test(filter = "leaky")

unlink("tests/testthat/test-leaky.R")

Source: testthat package documentation: set_state_inspector

ℹ Testing shelf
shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days
✔ | F W  S  OK | Context

✔ |   2      3 | leaky
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Warning ('test-leaky.R:6:1'): a test that leaks an option
Global state has changed:
`before$digits`: 7
 `after$digits`: 4

Warning ('test-leaky.R:11:1'): a test that leaks an environment variable
Global state has changed:
`before$shelf_env`: NA
`after$shelf_env`:  "leak"
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

══ Results ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
[ FAIL 0 | WARN 2 | SKIP 0 | PASS 3 ]

Source: testthat package documentation: Test fixtures

Each warning carries the location of the test (test-leaky.R:6:1, the line of the test_that() call), the word Global state has changed and the difference found by waldo, with the value before and after. The polite test, which used withr::local_options(), is not reported. A test file that is run in parallel inherits the state of the previous file in the same worker, so the inspector is also the tool for the stochastic failures that parallel testing can expose.

Mocking with local_mocked_bindings()

Mocking means temporarily replacing a function by a fake that behaves in a way the test controls. The reasons are the ones in the mocking article of testthat: to reach a failure that is hard to produce on purpose (what if a package is missing?), to make a test faster (replace a slow computation), and to make a test reliable (replace the clock, the network, the contents of a file). The same article is frank about the cost: mocking is an advanced technique that can make tests brittle, or let them hide problems, and should be used only when a simpler technique does not work.

In shelf there is exactly one mock, and it is a good example of the situation. overdue_loans() takes the reference date as an argument, today, which makes nearly all the tests deterministic without any mock. Its default, shelf_today(), is a one-line internal function that returns the current date: the code that reads the clock is in one place, behind a name that a test can replace.

The function is defined in R/loans.R with a comment that says why it exists ("kept as a function so that tests can replace it"), and its body is a single call of the base function Sys.Date.

The test that uses it is the second one of test-loans.R (shown in full above):

test_that("overdue_loans() uses the current date by default", {
  local_mocked_bindings(shelf_today = function() shelf_fixed_today)
  expect_identical(
    overdue_loans(loans),
    overdue_loans(loans, today = shelf_fixed_today)
  )
})

Source: testthat package documentation: local_mocked_bindings

local_mocked_bindings(shelf_today = function() shelf_fixed_today) replaces the binding shelf_today in the namespace of the package under test, for the length of the test; at the end of the test the original is put back. No .package argument is needed here: when a whole package’s tests are run, or when one package is loaded with devtools::load_all(), testthat knows which package is meant. Outside a package, in a script, it must be named.

How the replacement works

local_mocked_bindings() changes the binding in the package’s namespace environment, where the package’s own functions find their free variables (see Packages, Libraries and Namespaces for what a namespace is and Scoping, Environments and Closures for lexical scoping). Code in the package that calls shelf_today() sees the replacement; code elsewhere is not affected, which is the property testthat calls hygiene. Three consequences follow from that, and each shows up in the script below:

  • An unexported function cannot be reached as shelf::shelf_today(); the :: operator reports that it is not exported, and ::: reaches it. The script prints both.

  • Only a binding that already exists can be replaced. The namespace of a package is locked once it is loaded, so a new binding cannot be added, and local_mocked_bindings() reports a missing binding.

  • A function that belongs to base R, such as Sys.Date, has no binding in the package namespace and so cannot be replaced there. The remedies are either to put a placeholder binding for the base function in the package (interactive <- NULL is the example of the help page), or, as shelf does, to wrap the call in a function of the package, which is also better design. A function that the package calls as otherpackage::fun() is not read from the package namespace either; import it or call it through a wrapper that can be mocked.

The binding can be anything, not only a function (since testthat 3.2.1). Bindings in the imports of the package are also replaced, and so are S3 methods (since 3.1.8). with_mocked_bindings(code, ...) is the same replacement for one expression instead of the rest of the current scope.

library(testthat)
set_reporter(StopReporter$new(praise = FALSE))
loans <- shelf::loans

# shelf_today() is internal: shelf:: cannot reach it, shelf::: can.
tryCatch(shelf::shelf_today(), error = \(e) conditionMessage(e))
#> [1] "'shelf_today' is not an exported object from 'namespace:shelf'"
inherits(shelf:::shelf_today(), "Date")
#> [1] TRUE

# Which environment owns the function? The package, until it is replaced.
owner <- \() environmentName(environment(shelf:::shelf_today))
owner()
#> [1] "shelf"

# Outside the package's own tests, name the package whose binding to mock.
test_that("shelf_today() can be replaced for one test", {
  local_mocked_bindings(
    shelf_today = \() as.Date("2026-06-30"),
    .package = "shelf"
  )
  expect_identical(shelf:::shelf_today(), as.Date("2026-06-30"))
  print(owner())
  expect_identical(nrow(shelf::overdue_loans(loans)), 32L)
})
#> [1] ""

# After the test the original function is back.
owner()
#> [1] "shelf"

# The same replacement for a block of code only.
with_mocked_bindings(
  nrow(shelf::overdue_loans(loans)),
  shelf_today = \() as.Date("2026-06-30"),
  .package = "shelf"
)
#> [1] 32

# Only bindings that already exist can be mocked.
tryCatch(
  local_mocked_bindings(not_a_function = \() 1, .package = "shelf"),
  error = \(e) conditionMessage(e)
)
#> [1] "Can't find binding for `not_a_function`"

# Base functions such as Sys.Date are not bindings of the package namespace.
tryCatch(
  local_mocked_bindings(
    Sys.Date = \() as.Date("2026-06-30"),
    .package = "shelf"
  ),
  error = \(e) conditionMessage(e)
)
#> [1] "Can't find binding for `Sys.Date`"

# A mock that returns different values in turn, such as answers to a prompt.
test_that("mock_output_sequence() returns its values one at a time", {
  answer <- mock_output_sequence("3", "n")
  expect_identical(answer(), "3")
  expect_identical(answer(), "n")
  expect_error(answer(), "Can't find value for 3th iteration")
})

Source: testthat package documentation: local_mocked_bindings and with_mocked_bindings

The first call prints the real text of the error that :: gives for an internal function; the next line shows ::: working. owner() asks which environment the function belongs to: before the test it is the package ("shelf"). Inside the test, shelf:::shelf_today() returns the fixed date, owner() prints an empty name (the replacement is a function created inside the test, whose environment has no name), and overdue_loans(loans), called with no today argument, finds the 32 overdue loans that today = shelf_fixed_today found in the real test. After the test owner() is "shelf" again: the original function is back. with_mocked_bindings() returns the value of its expression (32). The next two calls are the real messages for the two mistakes above. The last test shows mock_output_sequence(), which creates a function that returns its arguments one at a time, for code that asks for several answers (a prompt, a retried request); asking for more values than it holds is an error, caught by expect_error().

Other mocks, and alternatives

testthat 3.3.0 added local_mocked_s3_method(), local_mocked_s4_method() and local_mocked_r6_class() for methods and classes, and 3.3.2 let the S3 and S4 versions mock methods that do not exist yet or remove one temporarily. The mocking article says to reach for them once the basic idea is clear and not before.

The older with_mock() and local_mock() replaced functions by modifying the namespace of a package. The NEWS of testthat deprecated them in 3.0.0, recommending the mockr or mockery packages instead, and made them defunct in 3.3.0, because the technique that made them work is no longer permitted in R 4.5.0; the message that the script of the third-edition section printed for with_mock() is "with_mock() was deprecated in testthat 3.2.0 and is now defunct" followed by the advice to use with_mocked_bindings(). Those two packages, which were the recommendation before local_mocked_bindings() existed, are not used on this page; neither is installed in the image used here.

Before mocking, three designs remove the need for it, and tests written that way are simpler to read:

  • Make the state an argument. overdue_loans(loans, today = ...) and loan_summary(loans, books, today, loan_days) take the date and the loan period as parameters with defaults, so a test passes the values it wants.

  • Make the global state a package option read at call time, as shelf.loan_days is, and change it for one test with withr::local_options().

  • Separate computation from input and output, so the part under test is a pure function (see Writing code that is easy to test).

Mocking is the right tool when none of those fits: a failure that cannot be provoked (the network is down), a slow or non-deterministic dependency, an interactive prompt, a platform check. Keep the replacement as small as possible, and test the real thing too wherever you can.

Skipping tests

A skipped test is neither a pass nor a failure: it is a test that cannot or should not run in the current circumstances, and the reporter says why. The cases the skipping article lists are the usual ones. The test depends on a web service that sometimes fails, or on credentials that exist only on some machines. It uses a feature that some operating systems lack (Windows, for example, has had limited UTF-8 support). It needs a version of R or of a dependency that not every test machine has. Or it is simply too slow for the CRAN check farm, whose policy asks that checking a package should take as little CPU time as possible, that long-running tests may be made optional, and that a package which uses Internet resources should fail gracefully, with an informative message and without a check warning or error, when the resource is unavailable.

Source: CRAN Repository Policy

skip(message) signals a condition of class skip; test_that() catches it, abandons the rest of the block and reports the reason. The helper functions call skip() for you when a condition holds:

Function Skips when

skip_if(condition, message), skip_if_not(condition, message)

The condition is TRUE (skip_if()) or not TRUE (skip_if_not()): the building blocks for your own helpers.

skip_if_not_installed(pkg, minimum_version)

The package is not installed or cannot be loaded, or is older than minimum_version.

skip_unless_r(">= 4.1.0")

The running R does not satisfy the specification (testthat 3.3.0).

skip_on_cran(), local_on_cran()

The tests count as running on CRAN: NOT_CRAN is set to something other than true, or it is unset and the session is not interactive. local_on_cran(TRUE) pretends to be on CRAN for the current scope (3.3.0).

skip_on_os(os, arch)

The operating system ("windows", "mac", "linux", "solaris", "emscripten") and, optionally, the architecture match.

skip_on_ci()

The environment variable CI is set, as continuous-integration services do.

skip_on_covr()

covr is measuring coverage (the environment variable R_COVR is set).

skip_on_bioc()

The check runs on a Bioconductor build machine (IS_BIOC_BUILD_MACHINE).

skip_if_offline(host)

There is no internet connection; needs the curl package, and itself calls skip_on_cran().

skip_if_translated(msgid)

The message identified by msgid is translated in the current language.

Source: testthat package documentation: skip

The script catches the skip condition with tryCatch() (a skip is a condition, see Conditions and Error Handling) and prints the reason that each helper would have given. The helper reason() returns "not skipped" when the code ran to the end:

library(testthat)

# A skip is a condition of class "skip": catch it to read the reason.
reason <- \(code) {
  tryCatch(
    {
      code
      "not skipped"
    },
    skip = \(s) conditionMessage(s)
  )
}

reason(skip("the catalogue server is down"))
#> [1] "Reason: the catalogue server is down"
reason(skip_if(TRUE, "RUN_SLOW_TESTS is not set"))
#> [1] "Reason: RUN_SLOW_TESTS is not set"
reason(skip_if_not(FALSE))
#> [1] "Reason: FALSE is not TRUE"
reason(skip_if_not(file.exists("secure-token.json"), "no token"))
#> [1] "Reason: no token"
reason(skip_if_not_installed("nosuchpackage"))
#> [1] "Reason: {nosuchpackage} is not installed"
reason(skip_if_not_installed("testthat", minimum_version = "99.0.0"))
#> [1] "Reason: Installed testthat is version 3.3.2; but 99.0.0 is required"
reason(skip_on_os("windows"))
#> [1] "not skipped"
reason(skip_unless_r(">= 99.0"))
#> [1] "Reason: Current R version (4.6.1) does not satisfy requirement (>= 99.0)"
reason(skip_on_cran())
#> [1] "Reason: On CRAN"
reason(skip_on_ci())
#> [1] "not skipped"

# skip_on_cran() looks at NOT_CRAN, which devtools and testthat set to "true".
Sys.getenv("NOT_CRAN", "<unset>")
#> [1] "<unset>"
Sys.setenv(NOT_CRAN = "false")
reason(skip_on_cran())
#> [1] "Reason: On CRAN"
Sys.setenv(NOT_CRAN = "true")
reason(skip_on_cran())
#> [1] "not skipped"

# local_on_cran() pretends to be on CRAN until the current scope ends.
local({
  local_on_cran(TRUE)
  reason(skip_on_cran())
})
#> [1] "Reason: On CRAN"
reason(skip_on_cran())
#> [1] "not skipped"

# skip_on_ci() looks at CI.
Sys.setenv(CI = "true")
reason(skip_on_ci())
#> [1] "Reason: On CI"

Source: testthat package documentation: Skipping tests

Notice what each line says. skip_if_not(FALSE) has no message of its own, and the reason is the generated FALSE is not TRUE. skip_if_not_installed() writes the package name in braces and, for a version requirement, both versions. skip_unless_r() prints the running version of R next to the requirement. The three helpers whose answer depends on the environment (skip_on_cran(), skip_on_ci(), skip_on_os()) give different answers on different machines, which is the point, but also the reason to be careful. In a plain Rscript session NOT_CRAN is not set, so skip_on_cran() already reports On CRAN, as it does on the check farm; the variable NOT_CRAN=true is what turns it off, and devtools::test() and testthat::test_local() set it when it is not set already (the table in Running tests shows which test function does what). Setting NOT_CRAN to "false" skips, "true" does not, and local_on_cran(TRUE) pretends to be on CRAN until the end of its scope, which is how you rehearse a CRAN run from an interactive session.

What a skip looks like in a report

The reporters count the skips and, since testthat 3.0.0, list them by reason at the end, so that a suite which silently skips half of its tests is visible. The scratch file below has four tests that skip for four reasons, one that has no expectation at all (which test_that() reports as a skip with the reason empty test), and one that runs:

# A scratch test file that skips for several reasons.
writeLines(
  trimws(r"---(
test_that("a test that needs a service", {
  skip("the catalogue server is down")
  expect_true(FALSE)
})

test_that("a test that needs a suggested package", {
  skip_if_not_installed("nosuchpackage")
  expect_true(FALSE)
})

test_that("a test for newer versions of R only", {
  skip_unless_r(">= 99.0.0")
  expect_true(FALSE)
})

test_that("a test that runs everywhere", {
  skip_on_os("windows")
  expect_true(TRUE)
})

test_that("a test that has not been written yet", {
  x <- 1
})
)---", whitespace = "\n"),
  "tests/testthat/test-skips.R"
)

devtools::test(filter = "skips")

unlink("tests/testthat/test-skips.R")

Source: testthat package documentation: skip

ℹ Testing shelf
shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days
✔ | F W  S  OK | Context

✔ |      4   1 | skips

══ Results ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
── Skipped tests (4) ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• {nosuchpackage} is not installed (1): 'test-skips.R:7:3'
• Current R version (4.6.1) does not satisfy requirement (>= 99.0.0) (1):
  'test-skips.R:12:3'
• empty test (1): 'test-skips.R:21:1'
• the catalogue server is down (1): 'test-skips.R:2:3'

[ FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 4 | PASS 1 ]

Source: testthat package documentation: Skipping tests

The summary after the results has one line for each reason, with the number of tests and the places in the file; the progress line for the file has 4 in the skip column and 1 in the passes. The skipped test with the reason empty test is the one that has no expectations.

shelf has two tests that skip on CRAN: the long check at the end of test-loans.R, which calls skip_on_cran(), and the snapshot test of test-book.R, which skips itself because snapshot expectations return without checking when NOT_CRAN is not true (see Snapshots and CRAN). The effect on a real check is shown in Tests under R CMD check: [ FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 2 | PASS 49 ] without NOT_CRAN and [ FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 0 | PASS 52 ] with it.

Writing skip helpers, and when not to skip

A skip condition that several tests share belongs in a helper whose name starts with skip_, in a helper-*.R file. The fragment below is an example and not a script, and shelf has no such file:

skip_if_no_token <- function() {
  skip_if_not(file.exists("secure-token.json"), "no token")
}

Source: testthat package documentation: Skipping tests

Another technique from the same article is to put a skip() inside a package function that cannot work without some tool, guarded by testthat::is_testing() (or the environment variable TESTTHAT, set to true while tests run), so that the function raises its normal error for users and a skip for the tests; the authors say they have mixed feelings about it, because it mixes code and tests.

Skipping is a decision with a cost. A skipped test is not a tested feature, and the usual way to fool yourself is to skip so much on CRAN or CI that the part of the suite that does run proves little. The advice in the article is to keep an eye on the skip summary. Three more points follow from this page. Do not skip because a suggested package is not installed: since testthat 3.3.0, test_that() does that by itself on CRAN, and the article advises assuming suggested packages are present except where they are hard to install. Do not use skip_on_os() to avoid a portability bug; fix the code. And if a test is slow, think about a smaller input before skip_on_cran(): the shelf test that is skipped on CRAN multiplies the loans fifty times to make the input large, and a smaller multiple would test the same thing.

The third edition: Config/testthat/edition and local_edition()

testthat has a very large number of reverse dependencies, and changing the behaviour of expect_equal() or of expect_warning() would turn passing test suites on CRAN into failing ones. testthat 3.0.0 (2020-10-31) therefore introduced the idea of an edition: a bundle of behaviours that a package must choose explicitly. A package that does not choose keeps the second edition, the behaviour of testthat 2.x; a package that chooses the third edition gets the current recommendations. The authors say that a new edition will be rare and will come with a new major version, so a fourth edition would arrive with testthat 4.0.0, and they explain why a new edition is not a new major version number: CRAN checks every package that uses testthat with the latest testthat, so incrementing the major version alone would not protect anyone from failures.

The edition is chosen in three places, from the widest to the narrowest.

  • In DESCRIPTION, for every test of the package: Config/testthat/edition: 3. usethis::use_testthat(3) writes this field, together with the version requirement testthat (>= 3.0.0) in Suggests, as the listing of the shelf package earlier on this page shows.

  • In a test file or a test, with local_edition(3) (or local_edition(2) to go back for one test while upgrading a suite). The change lasts until the current scope ends. edition_get() returns the edition in force.

  • With the environment variable TESTTHAT_EDITION, which testthat 3.0.3 added: handy for scripts that run outside a package, because outside a package there is no DESCRIPTION to read, and the answer is then the second edition. This is why the scripts of this page that call third-edition behaviour start with Sys.setenv(TESTTHAT_EDITION = "3"), and why edition_get() in the script below prints 2.

Source: testthat package documentation: testthat 3e

The third edition makes three kinds of change, and the scripts show each of them side by side with the second edition.

  • Equality is compared by waldo. expect_equal() and expect_identical() call waldo::compare() instead of all.equal() and identical(). The difference is in what a failure tells you, as the first part of the script shows with two factors that have different levels. The second edition reports Attributes: < Component “levels”: Lengths (2, 3) differ (string compare on first 2) >, which is the message of all.equal(); the third reports the two level vectors one under the other with the names levels(actual) and levels(expected). Besides the display, three behaviours differ: a single definition of tolerance everywhere (the old code mixed all.equal() and testthat’s own compare()), the environments of functions and formulas are compared unless ignore_function_env or ignore_formula_env is set (this matters when testing fitted models), and a time zone that is set implicitly differs from one that is set explicitly.

  • Warnings and messages are captured one at a time and nothing is swallowed. In the second edition expect_warning() swallowed every warning in the code, matching or not. In the third it captures at most one warning, the first that matches regexp and class, and every other warning bubbles up, so the second warning of warn_twice() is reported in the test (with the backtrace in the output). The same holds for expect_error(), expect_message() and expect_condition(), which use the same logic. Messages are no longer silenced automatically: the text reading the catalogue printed by chatty() appears in the output of the third-edition test and not in that of the second. Silence them with suppressMessages(), or test them with expect_message().

  • Outdated functions are deprecated. They still run, but each one warns, so the warnings tell you what to change; they do not make R CMD check fail.

library(testthat)
set_reporter(StopReporter$new(praise = FALSE))

# Outside a package there is no DESCRIPTION, so the 2nd edition is active.
edition_get()
#> [1] 2

# Equality: all.equal() in the 2nd edition, waldo in the 3rd.
a <- factor(c("fiction", "poetry"))
b <- factor(c("fiction", "poetry"), levels = c("fiction", "poetry", "classic"))
compare_in <- \(edition) {
  tryCatch(
    test_that(paste("factors in edition", edition), {
      local_edition(edition)
      expect_equal(a, b)
    }),
    error = \(e) invisible(NULL)
  )
}
compare_in(2)
#> ── Failure: factors in edition 2 ───────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Expected `a` to equal `b`.
#> Differences:
#> Attributes: < Component “levels”: Lengths (2, 3) differ (string compare on first 2) >
compare_in(3)
#> ── Failure: factors in edition 3 ───────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Expected `a` to equal `b`.
#> Differences:
#> `levels(actual)`:   "fiction" "poetry"
#> `levels(expected)`: "fiction" "poetry" "classic"
#>

# Warnings: the 2nd edition swallows every warning, the 3rd captures one.
warn_twice <- \() {
  warning("first")
  warning("second")
}
test_that("warnings in edition 2", {
  local_edition(2)
  expect_warning(warn_twice(), "first")
})
test_that("warnings in edition 3", {
  local_edition(3)
  expect_warning(warn_twice(), "first")
})
#> ── Warning: warnings in edition 3 ──────────────────────────────────────────────
#> second
#> Backtrace:
#>     ▆
#>  1. ├─testthat::expect_warning(warn_twice(), "first")
#>  2. │ └─testthat:::expect_condition_matching_(...)
#>  3. │   └─testthat:::quasi_capture(...)
#>  4. │     ├─testthat (local) .capture(...)
#>  5. │     │ └─base::withCallingHandlers(...)
#>  6. │     └─rlang::eval_bare(quo_get_expr(.quo), quo_get_env(.quo))
#>  7. └─global warn_twice()

# Messages: silenced in the 2nd edition, shown in the 3rd.
chatty <- \() {
  message("reading the catalogue")
  16L
}
test_that("messages in edition 2", {
  local_edition(2)
  expect_equal(chatty(), 16L)
})
test_that("messages in edition 3", {
  local_edition(3)
  expect_equal(chatty(), 16L)
})
#> reading the catalogue

Source: testthat package documentation: local_edition

The script ran with the second edition in force, because outside a package nothing selects the third. Each comparison is made inside a test_that() block, with local_edition(edition) as its first line. The failure of the second-edition factor test, the same failure in the third edition, the warning second that escapes the third-edition expect_warning() (with its backtrace, which shows that it was raised by the call warn_twice() in the test), and the message reading the catalogue that appears only once are all the real output of the script. The order of the lines in a captured log can differ from the order in which the text was produced, because messages and warnings go to the error stream and results to the standard output.

The deprecated functions

The functions that the third edition deprecates are the ones that its own article lists. Run in the third edition, each one warns with the replacement to use, and the script below catches the warning to print its text:

library(testthat)
Sys.setenv(TESTTHAT_EDITION = "3")
source("scenario.R")

# In the 3rd edition the old helpers still run, but each one warns.
deprecation <- \(code) {
  tryCatch({
    code
    "no warning"
  }, warning = \(w) conditionMessage(w))
}

b <- book("Salt and Static", "Mara Quill", year = 2018)
deprecation(expect_is(b, "book"))
#> [1] "`expect_is()` was deprecated in the 3rd edition.\nℹ Use `expect_type()`, `expect_s3_class()`, or `expect_s4_class()` instead"
deprecation(expect_equivalent(c(a = 1), 1))
#> [1] "`expect_equivalent()` was deprecated in the 3rd edition.\nℹ Use expect_equal(ignore_attr = TRUE)"
deprecation(context("book"))
#> [1] "`context()` was deprecated in the 3rd edition."
deprecation(setup(NULL))
#> [1] "`setup()` was deprecated in the 3rd edition.\nℹ Please use test fixtures instead see vignette('test-fixtures') for details"
deprecation(teardown(NULL))
#> [1] "`teardown()` was deprecated in the 3rd edition.\nℹ Please use test fixtures instead see vignette('test-fixtures') for details"
deprecation(expect_that(1, equals(1)))
#> [1] "`expect_that()` was deprecated in the 3rd edition."
deprecation(expect_known_value(1, tempfile()))
#> [1] "`expect_known_value()` was deprecated in the 3rd edition.\nℹ Please use `expect_snapshot_value()` instead"

# with_mock() and local_mock() were removed in testthat 3.3.0.
tryCatch(with_mock(sqrt = \(x) 0, sqrt(4)), error = \(e) conditionMessage(e))
#> [1] "`with_mock()` was deprecated in testthat 3.2.0 and is now defunct.\nℹ Please use `with_mocked_bindings()` instead."

Source: testthat package documentation: testthat 3e

The replacements, in the order of the output, are: expect_type(), expect_s3_class() or expect_s4_class() for expect_is() (it forces you to say which object system you mean); expect_equal(ignore_attr = TRUE) for expect_equivalent(); nothing for context(), because the file name already serves as the context; test fixtures instead of setup() and teardown() (see Fixtures and withr); plain expectations instead of the very old expect_that(x, equals(y)) syntax; and snapshots (expect_snapshot_value() and its relatives) for expect_known_value(), expect_known_output(), expect_known_hash() and expect_equal_to_reference(). The last line of the output is not a warning but an error: with_mock() and local_mock(), deprecated for a long time, are defunct since testthat 3.3.0, and the message points to with_mocked_bindings() (see Mocking). Some other changes of the third edition are described elsewhere on this page: the condition expectations return the condition, not the value of the code (testthat 3.1.0, a change that applies to the third edition only), expect_snapshot() requires the third edition, and parallel testing requires it as well.

Reproducible output

test_that() and it() call local_test_context() at the start of each test. It sets the environment variable TESTTHAT to true (in both editions) and, in the third edition only, calls local_reproducible_output(), which makes printed output the same on every machine: it turns off colour and cli Unicode bullets, sets the console width to 80, the collation to C, the language to C (to disable translations; this was "en" before testthat 3.2.2), max.print to its default, and so on. These are the arguments of the function and their defaults: width = 80, crayon = FALSE, unicode = FALSE, rstudio = FALSE, hyperlinks = FALSE, lang = "C". A test that needs something else asks for it with local_reproducible_output(width = 40). The script prints the values outside a test, inside, and inside a test that changes the width:

library(testthat)
Sys.setenv(TESTTHAT_EDITION = "3")
set_reporter(StopReporter$new(praise = FALSE))

# Outside a test.
c(Sys.getenv("TESTTHAT", "<unset>"), getOption("width"), is_testing())
#> [1] "<unset>" "80"      "FALSE"

# Inside test_that() testthat makes the output reproducible.
test_that("tests run in a controlled context", {
  cat("TESTTHAT:", Sys.getenv("TESTTHAT"), "\n")
  cat("width:", getOption("width"), "\n")
  cat("unicode:", getOption("cli.unicode"), "\n")
  cat("collation:", Sys.getlocale("LC_COLLATE"), "\n")
  expect_true(is_testing())
  expect_false(is_checking())
  expect_false(is_snapshot())
})
#> TESTTHAT: true
#> width: 80
#> unicode: FALSE
#> collation: C

# local_reproducible_output() lets one test ask for something else.
test_that("a test can change the console width", {
  local_reproducible_output(width = 40L)
  cat("width:", getOption("width"), "\n")
  expect_identical(getOption("width"), 40L)
})
#> width: 40

Source: testthat package documentation: local_test_context

Outside a test the width is 80, R’s default; Sys.getenv("TESTTHAT") is <unset> and is_testing() is FALSE. Inside the test TESTTHAT is true, cli.unicode is FALSE and the collation is C, whatever the machine’s locale is. The three predicates is_testing(), is_checking() and is_snapshot() (testthat 3.1.9 for the last two) tell code whether it runs in tests, in a test run by R CMD check, or inside a snapshot. is_parallel() tells whether the files are run in worker processes. They exist for the few cases where a package function really has to behave differently under test.

Upgrading a suite from the second edition

The upgrade has four steps, in the order of the third-edition article. Activate the edition (usethis::use_testthat(3) does it). Replace or remove the deprecated functions. If the output became noisy, capture or suppress the warnings and messages that were silently swallowed before. Then inspect the tests that fail because the objects are no longer "all equal"; use local_edition(2) in a test that needs more time, and remove it afterwards. Tests that call expect_equal() on models, formulas or functions are the ones most likely to need a change.

Running tests

The same test files can be run in several ways, and the ways differ in what they load, which reporter they use, whether they assume the tests are not on CRAN and whether a failure is an error. The package source is loaded with pkgload::load_all() (pkgload 1.5.3), the function behind devtools::load_all(), in the development workflows, and the installed package is used in the checking workflows.

Function Purpose Loads the package Defaults

devtools::test()

The everyday command in a package directory. Saves open files, runs test_local() with the environment variables of a development session, including NOT_CRAN=true when it is unset.

from source, with all functions visible (export_all = TRUE)

progress reporter; a failing test does not raise an error (stop_on_failure = FALSE)

devtools::test_active_file()

Runs the test file that is open in the editor (or the test file that belongs to the open source file)

from source

compact reporter for a single file

testthat::test_local(path)

devtools::test() without devtools: the same test directory, run for a source package, assuming not on CRAN

from source (load_package = "source")

progress reporter; a failure is an error

testthat::test_dir(path, filter, package, load_package)

The low-level function behind the others. Runs every test-*.R of a directory, after the helpers and setup files

load_package = "none" (the default), "installed" or "source"

progress reporter, or the parallel one; a failure is an error

testthat::test_file(path, desc)

One file, or one test of it

as test_dir()

compact reporter

testthat::test_check(package)

What tests/testthat.R calls under R CMD check

the installed package, attached with library()

check reporter; a failure is an error

testthat::test_package(package)

The tests of an installed package, if the tests were installed with it

installed

check reporter

Source: testthat package documentation: test_package, test_check and test_local

Three arguments are worth knowing. filter of test_dir() and its relatives is a regular expression matched against the file name after test- and .R have been removed: filter = "loans|clean" runs test-loans.R and test-clean.R, and a pattern that matches nothing is an error, No test files found.. desc of test_file() (testthat 3.2.0) runs one test of a file, selected by its description; since 3.3.0 it can be a character vector that names the path through nested describe() blocks. And shuffle = TRUE (testthat 3.3.0) randomly reorders the top-level expressions of each file, which is a way to find tests that depend on the order in which they run.

Source: testthat package documentation: test_dir

From the console: test_file(), test_dir() and test_local()

The script runs parts of the suite of shelf in five ways, with the check reporter for the first four so that the output is compact. It must be run from the package directory. Two things in it deserve attention. test_file() and test_dir() do not load the package by themselves, so the calls give package = "shelf" and load_package = "source". And test_dir() does not set NOT_CRAN, so in the third call the test that calls skip_on_cran() is skipped, whereas test_local() in the fourth call assumes a development session and runs it.

library(testthat)

# One file: load the package from source first (test_file() does not).
test_file(
  "tests/testthat/test-clean.R",
  package = "shelf", load_package = "source", reporter = "check"
)

# One test of a file (testthat 3.2.0 and later), found by its description.
test_file(
  "tests/testthat/test-book.R",
  desc = "validate_book() rejects bad values with a clear message",
  package = "shelf", load_package = "source", reporter = "check"
)

# A directory, filtered by the part of the file name after "test-".
# test_dir() does not set NOT_CRAN, so the skip_on_cran() test is skipped.
test_dir(
  "tests/testthat", filter = "loans|clean",
  package = "shelf", load_package = "source", reporter = "check"
)

# test_local() is devtools::test() without devtools: it assumes not on CRAN.
test_local(".", filter = "loans|clean", reporter = "check")

# The value is a testthat_results list that converts to a data frame.
res <- test_local(".", filter = "book", reporter = "silent")
class(res)
head(as.data.frame(res)[, c("file", "nb", "failed", "skipped")], 3L)

Source: testthat package documentation: test_file

[ FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 0 | PASS 4 ]

1 test-book.R  7      0   FALSE

Source: testthat package documentation: test_dir

Read the totals in order. The first run, of test-clean.R, has 14 passing expectations, as the file has (PASS 14). The second runs the single test selected by its desc: PASS 4. The third runs the files whose names match loans|clean: 27 expectations pass and 1 test is skipped, with the report of the skip (On CRAN, with the location of the test in the file). The fourth, test_local(), runs the same files and nothing is skipped: PASS 28. The last lines show what the functions return: an object of class testthat_results, a list that as.data.frame() turns into one row per test with the file, the number of expectations (nb), whether any failed or was skipped, the warnings and the timings. The script prints only the file, nb, failed and skipped columns, because the timing columns differ from run to run.

Reporters

A reporter is the object that receives the results and decides what to print. Every function that runs several tests has a reporter argument that takes a name ("minimal") or an object (MinimalReporter$new()). The reference page of testthat lists these:

Reporter What it does

ProgressReporter ("progress")

The default of test_dir(): a table with one line for each file and columns for failures, warnings, skips and passes, redrawn as the tests run, then the details of every problem. Since testthat 3.1.9 it re-displays all failures at the end and lists skips only at the end.

ParallelProgressReporter

The default when the files run in parallel.

CompactProgressReporter

The default of test_file(): the progress reporter tuned for a single file.

CheckReporter ("check")

For R CMD check: designed to show something useful in the last 13 lines that the check log keeps. It prints all the problems, errors, failures, warnings and skips, and not only the first ten, and lists skips by reason.

SummaryReporter, MinimalReporter, LocationReporter

A summary of failures for interactive use; one character per expectation, . for success; the location of every expectation and error, useful when you look for the test that crashes R or hangs.

StopReporter

The reporter of a test_that() call run directly: it displays the result and stops with an error if the test has failures. The scripts at the top of this page use it.

TapReporter, JunitReporter, TeamcityReporter

Machine-readable output: the Test Anything Protocol, jUnit XML (needs the xml2 package; read by CI dashboards such as Jenkins) and TeamCity messages.

ListReporter, SilentReporter, MultiReporter, FailReporter

Collect the results without printing; do nothing visible; run several reporters at once; throw an error at the end if any test failed. reporter = c("check", "fail") is the way to get a failing exit status from a reporter that does not fail.

SlowReporter ("slow")

Reports the time of each test and filters out the fast ones (default threshold 1 second); testthat 3.3.0.

DebugReporter, RStudioReporter, LlmReporter

Call recover() at each failure; produce output for the RStudio IDE; report problems as they occur and the number of successes at the end, for coding agents. The default is chosen automatically when tests are run by Claude Code, Cursor or Gemini CLI; other agents set AGENT=1 (testthat 3.3.2).

Source: testthat package documentation: Reporter

The default can be changed with the options testthat.default_reporter, testthat.default_parallel_reporter, testthat.default_compact_reporter and testthat.default_check_reporter. The script runs one small file with four reporters and prints a few lines of what each gives; the JUnit file is written to a temporary file and only the number of <testcase> elements is printed:

library(testthat)

run <- \(reporter) {
  test_local(".", filter = "clean", reporter = reporter)
}

# The one-line-per-expectation dot reporter.
invisible(run("minimal"))

# Where each expectation is, handy to find a hanging test.
out <- capture.output(invisible(run("location")))
head(out[nzchar(out)], 6L)

# What R CMD check shows: the counts, plus details only for problems.
invisible(run("check"))

# Machine-readable output: TAP, and JUnit XML for CI servers.
out <- capture.output(invisible(run("tap")))
head(out, 4L)
xml <- tempfile(fileext = ".xml")
invisible(run(JunitReporter$new(file = xml)))
sum(grepl("<testcase ", readLines(xml), fixed = TRUE))

Source: testthat package documentation: Reporter

The minimal reporter printed 14 dots, one per expectation. The location reporter printed Start test: and End test: lines around the location of every expectation, as 'test-clean.R:3:3' [success]; the first six lines are shown. The check reporter printed only the totals, because nothing went wrong. The TAP reporter’s first lines are the plan 1..14, then one ok line per expectation with the description of the test. The JUnit file has 14 test cases. The line shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days before each run is the startup message of the package, printed when load_all() attaches it.

Stopping early: set_max_fails()

A suite in which the same mistake breaks hundreds of expectations produces more output than anybody reads. The progress reporter stops a run after 10 failures; the limit is the option testthat.progress.max_fails or the environment variable TESTTHAT_MAX_FAILS, which set_max_fails() sets (for the current R process and any process it starts), and set_max_fails(Inf) removes it. The scratch file below sorts first, because its name starts with aaa, and fails twice:

# A scratch file that sorts before the others and fails twice.
writeLines(
  trimws(r"---(
test_that("first failure", expect_identical(1L, 2L))
test_that("second failure", expect_identical("a", "b"))
)---", whitespace = "\n"),
  "tests/testthat/test-aaa-failing.R"
)

# Stop after the first failing file instead of running everything.
testthat::set_max_fails(1L)
Sys.getenv("TESTTHAT_MAX_FAILS")
devtools::test()

# Inf lifts the limit again.
testthat::set_max_fails(Inf)
unlink("tests/testthat/test-aaa-failing.R")

Source: testthat package documentation: set_max_fails

✔ | F W  S  OK | Context

✖ | 2        0 | aaa-failing
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Expected 1L to be identical to 2L.
Differences:
  `actual`: 1
`expected`: 2


Failure ('test-aaa-failing.R:2:1'): second failure
Expected "a" to be identical to "b".
Differences:
`actual`:   "a"
`expected`: "b"

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Maximum number of failures exceeded; quitting.

Source: testthat package documentation: set_max_fails

The first line of the script’s output, "1", is the environment variable after set_max_fails(1L). Both failures of the scratch file are reported, because the progress reporter stops at the end of the file in which the limit is exceeded (since testthat 3.1.0), not in the middle of it, and the message Maximum number of failures exceeded; quitting. names the remedy. The remaining test files are not run, which is what the limit is for, and also why a failing run with a low limit says nothing about the tests that did not run.

Running in parallel

Test files can run in separate R processes. The conditions are the third edition and the line Config/testthat/parallel: true in DESCRIPTION. By default testthat uses getOption("Ncpus", 2) processes (the number of processes can be set with the environment variable TESTTHAT_CPUS, best put in .Renviron), and TESTTHAT_PARALLEL=false turns parallel running off temporarily, which is what to do for print debugging, because the output of print(), cat() and message() from the test files is lost when they run in a worker. A field Config/testthat/start-first lists glob patterns of test files to start first, so that the slowest ones begin early. Each worker loads testthat and the package, runs the setup files and then receives test files one at a time; state therefore persists between the files that one worker runs, which is the reason files must clean up after themselves (see Fixtures and withr). Packages with many fast test files gain little, because starting the workers and relaying the results costs time: the article gives the tests of testthat itself as an example, 10 seconds in serial and 8 in parallel. A test_dir() call on a single file runs in serial since testthat 3.3.2. Some reporters cannot work in parallel (the debug, JUnit and location reporters and the stop reporter), and testthat then runs the files serially.

# Switch parallel testing on in DESCRIPTION (and put it back at the end).
description <- readLines("DESCRIPTION")
writeLines(c(description, "Config/testthat/parallel: true"), "DESCRIPTION")
tail(readLines("DESCRIPTION"), 2L)

# Two worker processes; the "check" reporter prints only the totals.
Sys.setenv(TESTTHAT_CPUS = "2")
devtools::test(reporter = "check")

# TESTTHAT_PARALLEL=false runs the files in this process again.
Sys.setenv(TESTTHAT_PARALLEL = "false")
devtools::test(reporter = "check")

writeLines(description, "DESCRIPTION")

Source: testthat package documentation: Running tests in parallel
