Starting 2 test processes.
[ FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 0 | PASS 52 ]
ℹ Testing shelf
shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days
[ FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 0 | PASS 52 ]

Source: testthat package documentation: Running tests in parallel

The first line is the end of DESCRIPTION with the new field, then the real message Starting 2 test processes. appears, and the totals are the same PASS 52 as before. The second run, with TESTTHAT_PARALLEL set to false, runs in this process and prints the package startup message that the workers do not. The script restores DESCRIPTION at the end.

Environment variables and options

The behaviour of the test runners is controlled by a handful of environment variables. All are read by testthat or by the check tools of R, and the table says where each is documented.

Variable or option Effect Documented in

NOT_CRAN

true means "not on CRAN": skip_on_cran() does not skip. Set by devtools and test_local(). Unset, the tests count as being on CRAN unless the session is interactive.

testthat: skip_on_cran()

CI

true on continuous-integration services: skip_on_ci() skips, and new snapshots fail.

testthat: skip_on_ci(), NEWS 3.3.0

TESTTHAT

true while a test runs; is_testing() reads it.

testthat: Skipping tests

TESTTHAT_EDITION

Selects the edition without a DESCRIPTION field.

testthat NEWS 3.0.3

TESTTHAT_PARALLEL, TESTTHAT_CPUS

false turns parallel running off; the number of worker processes.

testthat: Running tests in parallel

TESTTHAT_MAX_FAILS, option testthat.progress.max_fails

Failures after which the progress reporter stops (default 10).

testthat: set_max_fails()

TESTTHAT_PROBLEMS

false turns off the _problems/ reprex files under R CMD check.

testthat NEWS 3.3.0

_R_CHECK_TESTS_NLINES_

Number of trailing lines of test output kept in the check log (default 13; 0 keeps all lines except the R preamble).

R Internals: Tools

_R_CHECK_SUGGESTS_ONLY_, _R_CHECK_FORCE_SUGGESTS_

Whether examples, tests and vignettes run with a temporary library holding only the declared packages (false by default, true for CRAN submission checks); whether a suggested package that is not available is an error (true by default, false for CRAN submission checks).

R Internals: Tools

Source: R Internals: Tools

Tests under R CMD check

Everything above ran the tests from a development session. The tests of a package are also run, without any of devtools, by R CMD check, which first builds the source package into a tarball and then checks it. The two commands for shelf are below; --no-manual is there because the image has no TeX installation, and the environment variable switches off the checks that need the network, since R CMD check --as-cran would otherwise contact CRAN while checking the package name (see Publishing to CRAN for that check):

R CMD build shelf
_R_CHECK_CRAN_INCOMING_REMOTE_=false R CMD check --as-cran --no-manual shelf_0.1.0.tar.gz

Source: Writing R Extensions: Checking packages

The log is long. Its first lines (version of R, platform, compiler, session charset and the time) are trimmed here, and so are the lines of the checks that are not about tests. Two steps matter for this page: checking for unstated dependencies in ‘tests’ (every package that the files under tests/ load with library() or :: must be declared in DESCRIPTION), and checking tests itself:

* checking for unstated dependencies in ‘tests’ ... OK
* checking tests ...
  Running ‘base-check.R’
  Comparing ‘base-check.Rout’ to ‘base-check.Rout.save’ ... OK
  Running ‘testthat.R’
 OK
* checking for unstated dependencies in vignettes ... OK
* DONE

Status: OK

Source: Writing R Extensions: Checking packages

Each file that is directly in tests/ is run in a separate R process, in a copy of the directory, with the installed package available; its output is written next to it as <name>.Rout. The test run is ERROR if a script stops with an error, and OK otherwise. Here two files ran. The first, base-check.R, is the plain-R test file of the section on base R below, which was added to the copy of the package for this run; its output was compared with a reference file. The second, testthat.R, is the driver of the suite. Its output is in shelf.Rcheck/tests/testthat.Rout, where the check directory keeps it, and the part that test_check() produced is:

sed -n '/^> test_check/,/^> proc.time/p' shelf.Rcheck/tests/testthat.Rout

Source: Writing R Extensions: Package subdirectories

> test_check("shelf")
[ FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 2 | PASS 49 ]

══ Skipped tests (2) ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
• On CRAN (2): 'test-book.R:39:1', 'test-loans.R:40:3'

[ FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 2 | PASS 49 ]
>

Source: testthat package documentation: test_check

The totals are not those of devtools::test(). [ FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 2 | PASS 49 ] means that two tests were skipped on CRAN, and the report names them: test-book.R:39:1, the test that contains the two snapshot expectations, and test-loans.R:40:3, the one that calls skip_on_cran(). The NOT_CRAN environment variable is not set in a check run, and R CMD check --as-cran is what CRAN does, so testthat acts as it would there. The 49 are the 52 expectations of the development run minus the expectation in the skipped long test and the two snapshot expectations, which returned without checking anything (the other two expectations of the snapshot test did run). A maintainer who wants the whole suite to run in the local check sets the variable. Everything else in the log is the same:

NOT_CRAN=true _R_CHECK_CRAN_INCOMING_REMOTE_=false R CMD check --as-cran --no-manual shelf_0.1.0.tar.gz

Source: testthat package documentation: skip_on_cran

> test_check("shelf")
[ FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 0 | PASS 52 ]
>

Source: testthat package documentation: skip_on_cran

With NOT_CRAN=true the same suite reports SKIP 0 and PASS 52, both the snapshots and the long test run, and the snapshot file _snaps/book.md is compared with the output. This is the check to run before a release (and what the continuous-integration workflow of the section on coverage does), and the other, without the variable, is the check CRAN runs. Both must pass. A suite that passes only with NOT_CRAN=true has hidden a problem in a skipped test; one that passes only without it has a test that depends on something the check farm does not have.

Three more things happen in a check run, all visible in the documentation of R and of testthat.

  • The number of lines kept. The check log of a failing test shows only the last 13 lines of the output, which is the default of _R_CHECK_TESTS_NLINES_ (0 keeps everything but the R preamble). The check reporter of testthat was designed so that those 13 lines are useful. The full output of a failed run is in tests/testthat.Rout.fail in the check directory. The section on reading a failure shows the log of a failing check.

  • Only declared packages. With --as-cran the variable _R_CHECK_SUGGESTS_ONLY_ is true, so tests run with a library that contains only the packages declared in DESCRIPTION. A test that uses a package that is not listed in Suggests fails in the check although it worked in the development session, where all your packages are installed (the first section of this page shows the real output of that case).

  • The time limit and the CPU time. The CRAN Repository Policy asks that checking take as little CPU time as possible, and that long-running tests be made optional. Parallel testing must respect the limit of two cores that the policy sets for a package that uses several threads or cores; testthat’s default of getOption("Ncpus", 2) workers keeps within it.

Source: CRAN Repository Policy

The tests of an installed package can also be run later with tools::testInstalledPackage(), the function that covr uses to run the tests under instrumentation, and R CMD check can take its tests from a non-standard directory with the option --test-dir: Writing R Extensions suggests inst/slowTests for slow tests, and names inst/testWithOracle and inst/randomTests as other examples.

Base R alternatives: tests/*.R, .Rout.save and stopifnot

testthat is a convention on top of a mechanism that R itself provides, and the mechanism works without it. Writing R Extensions describes it in one paragraph. The tests directory holds .R files; the results of running a file are written to a .Rout file; if there is a .Rout.save file with the same name, the two are compared, and differences are reported but do not cause an error. The directory is copied to the check area and the tests run with that copy as the working directory, with R_LIBS set so that library(shelf) finds the package installed for the check. The tests run in a vanilla R session and without a random-number seed, so tests that use random numbers must set one. An error in a script, such as a failed stopifnot(), makes the test run fail. That is the whole contract: a test is a script that stops with an error when something is wrong.

Source: Writing R Extensions: Package subdirectories

The script below writes such a file into the copy of the package, tests/base-check.R, and lists the tests directory. The file loads the package, asserts with stopifnot() that a known ISBN is valid, builds a book, prints it and its summary, and prints two numbers about the overdue loans. It is the style of test that many older packages, and the packages of R itself, use: a script that exercises the code, with the expected output stored next to it.

# A base-R test: a plain script in tests/, run by R CMD check.
writeLines(
  trimws(r"---(
library(shelf)

stopifnot(is_valid_isbn13("978-0-306-40615-7"))

b <- book("Salt and Static", "Mara Quill", "978-0-01-400145-3", 2018,
          "Mystery", 244)
print(b)
summary(b)

overdue <- overdue_loans(loans, today = as.Date("2026-06-30"))
nrow(overdue)
range(overdue$days_out)
)---", whitespace = "\n"),
  "tests/base-check.R"
)
list.files("tests")

Source: Writing R Extensions: Package subdirectories

[1] "base-check.R" "testthat"     "testthat.R"

Source: Writing R Extensions: Package subdirectories

The reference output is made by running the file the way R CMD check will, with R CMD BATCH --vanilla, and keeping the result under the name that the check looks for. This is the file that the command writes, without the start-up banner of R (which carries the version and the platform) and without the proc.time() call and the timings that R CMD BATCH appends:

cd shelf/tests
R CMD BATCH --vanilla base-check.R base-check.Rout.save

Source: R documentation: BATCH

> library(shelf)
shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days
>
> stopifnot(is_valid_isbn13("978-0-306-40615-7"))
>
> b <- book("Salt and Static", "Mara Quill", "978-0-01-400145-3", 2018,
+           "Mystery", 244)
> print(b)
<book> Salt and Static (Mara Quill, 2018)
> summary(b)
Book: Salt and Static
ISBN known: TRUE
Pages: 244
>
> overdue <- overdue_loans(loans, today = as.Date("2026-06-30"))
> nrow(overdue)
[1] 32
> range(overdue$days_out)
[1] 22 84

Source: R documentation: Rdiff

When R CMD check compares base-check.Rout with base-check.Rout.save, it uses tools::Rdiff(), which removes the startup banner, the timings that R CMD BATCH appends and the lines about loading packages from both files, maps fancy quotes to plain ones and compares the rest line by line. Text between the markers > ## IGNORE_RDIFF_BEGIN and > ## IGNORE_RDIFF_END is ignored. Writing R Extensions adds the cautions: the comparison is verbatim, so anything that varies between runs (version numbers of other packages that are printed when they load, numbers printed with too many digits, timings, rounding errors that are really zero) makes the check report a difference, and the comparison is made in the end user’s locale, so reference output should be ASCII. The check for shelf with the matching file was OK in the log above. If the expected value in the reference file is edited from 32 to 31 (an experiment on the copy of the package), the check reports the difference and carries on; the status becomes a NOTE, not an error:

* checking tests ...
  Running ‘base-check.R’
  Comparing ‘base-check.Rout’ to ‘base-check.Rout.save’ ...
19c19
< [1] 32
---
> [1] 31
  Running ‘testthat.R’
 NOTE
Status: 1 NOTE

Source: Writing R Extensions: Checking packages

The lines 19c19, < [1] 32 and > [1] 31 are the output of diff: line 19 of the new output has 32, line 19 of the reference has 31. Reference files are fragile, and that is the weak point of the approach: every change in a print method means regenerating the file.

stopifnot(), all.equal() and the tools package

For assertions inside the script, base R has stopifnot() and all.equal(), and the tools package has assertError() and assertWarning(). The script below runs them against the shelf scenario:

source("scenario.R")

# stopifnot(): silent when everything is TRUE, an error otherwise.
stopifnot(is_valid_isbn13("978-0-306-40615-7"), nrow(books) == 16L)
caught <- \(code) tryCatch(code, error = \(e) conditionMessage(e))
caught(stopifnot(nrow(books) == 20L))
#> [1] "nrow(books) == 20L is not TRUE"
caught(stopifnot("every ISBN must be valid" = all(is_valid_isbn13(books$isbn))))
#> [1] "every ISBN must be valid"
caught(stopifnot(all.equal(1, 1.1)))
#> [1] "1 and 1.1 are not equal:\n  Mean relative difference: 0.1"

# all.equal() describes the difference; identical() only says yes or no.
all.equal(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3)
#> [1] TRUE
all.equal(1, 1.1)
#> [1] "Mean relative difference: 0.1"
all.equal(c(a = 1), c(b = 1))
#> [1] "Names: 1 string mismatch"
identical(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3)
#> [1] FALSE
isTRUE(all.equal(100, 100.0000001))
#> [1] TRUE

# The tools package has assertions for conditions.
tools::assertError(book(""))
tools::assertWarning(as.integer("x"))
caught(tools::assertError(book("A title")))
#> [1] "Failed to get error in evaluating book(\"A title\")"
caught(tools::assertWarning(book("A title")))
#> [1] "Failed to get warning in evaluating book(\"A title\")"

Source: R documentation: stopifnot

  • stopifnot(...) is silent when every argument is TRUE; otherwise it stops with a message built from the failing expression: nrow(books) == 20L is not TRUE. Since R 4.0.0 an argument can be named, and the name is the message ("every ISBN must be valid" = all(...)), which makes the failure readable without a message in the code (R NEWS: Changes in R 4.0.0). Since R 3.5.0 the expressions can also be given in one braced block as exprs =. stopifnot(all.equal(1, 1.1)) shows a pitfall that stopifnot() softens: all.equal() returns either TRUE or a character string that describes the difference, so an expression such as if (all.equal(x, y)) is an error waiting to happen. stopifnot() has recognised a call to all.equal() since R 3.4.0 and reports its message (1 and 1.1 are not equal: followed by Mean relative difference: 0.1); anywhere else, write isTRUE(all.equal(x, y)).

  • all.equal() compares two objects with a tolerance (by default sqrt(.Machine$double.eps), about 1.5e-8, relative to the size of the numbers) and says how they differ: Names: 1 string mismatch. identical() says only yes or no, and is exact: identical(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3) is FALSE. These are the base R counterparts of expect_equal() and expect_identical(); in the third edition testthat uses waldo and not these two functions.

  • tools::assertError(expr) and tools::assertWarning(expr) evaluate expr and signal an error if no error (respectively no warning) occurred, with the message Failed to get error in evaluating .... Since R 4.0.0 they accept a classes argument to require a specific condition class. They are the base R counterparts of expect_error() and expect_warning().

The table puts the three approaches side by side:

Question Base R (tests/*.R) testthat tinytest

Assert something is true

stopifnot(x)

expect_true(x)

expect_true(x)

Equal within tolerance

stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(x, y)))

expect_equal(x, y)

expect_equal(x, y)

Exactly identical

stopifnot(identical(x, y))

expect_identical(x, y)

expect_identical(x, y)

An error with a message

tools::assertError(f()) (message not checked)

expect_error(f(), "text")

expect_error(f(), pattern = "text")

Printed output

.Rout.save

expect_output(), expect_snapshot()

expect_stdout()

Grouping and names

none (a script)

test_that("...", { })

none (a script)

On failure

the script stops at the first error

all expectations of all tests run, one report

all expectations of a file run, one report

Source: R documentation: all.equal

Base-R tests are enough for a small package, they have no dependency, and they are also what to reach for in a package that must not suggest testthat. Their weakness is the failure report: a script stops at the first error with a one-line message, with no summary and no way to run one test, and the reference output compares text and not values. testthat adds the structure, and tinytest takes a middle way.

tinytest in brief

tinytest 1.4.3 (an add-on package, installed in the scratch library of these examples) is a small testing framework built on the idea that a test file should be a plain script. In its words, a test file is an R script in which some or all statements express an expectation; there is no test_that() block. It imports only the base packages parallel and utils. Its expectation functions have the names of the testthat ones (expect_equal(), expect_error(), expect_true()) with different arguments: the regular expression of expect_error() is called pattern, and the equality uses all.equal(). A test file runs from top to bottom, every expectation is recorded and nothing stops at a failure; run_test_file() returns an object of class tinytests that all_pass() and summary() inspect. The script below writes a four-expectation test file to a temporary directory and runs it. (Because the examples of this page run in a package-less script, shelf:: calls stand in for the package that a real test file would load.)

# A tinytest file is a plain script of expect_*() calls: no test_that() blocks.
file <- file.path(tempdir(), "test_isbn.R")
writeLines(r"---(
expect_true(shelf::is_valid_isbn13("978-0-306-40615-7"))
expect_false(shelf::is_valid_isbn13(""))
expect_equal(shelf::normalise_isbn("978-0-306-40615-7"), "9780306406157")
expect_error(shelf::book(""), pattern = "a book needs a title")
)---", file)

out <- tinytest::run_test_file(file, verbose = 0L)
tinytest::all_pass(out)
#> [1] TRUE
summary(out)
#>
#> File          Results fails passes
#>   test_isbn.R       4     0      4
#>   Total             4     0      4

Source: tinytest package documentation: run_test_file

tinytest::setup_tinytest(pkgdir) prepares a package: it creates inst/tinytest/ with an example test file, creates tests/tinytest.R so that R CMD check runs the tests, and adds tinytest to Suggests. The experiment below runs it on a copy of the shelf package in a temporary directory and prints what it wrote; the real tests/testthat.R and its suite are not touched:

# Let tinytest set up a COPY of the package (the real one stays untouched).
copy <- file.path(tempdir(), "shelf")
dir.create(copy)
files <- list.files(all.files = TRUE, no.. = TRUE)
invisible(file.copy(files, copy, recursive = TRUE))
tinytest::setup_tinytest(copy, verbose = FALSE)

cat(readLines(file.path(copy, "tests", "tinytest.R")), sep = "\n")
grep("tinytest", readLines(file.path(copy, "DESCRIPTION")), value = TRUE)
list.files(file.path(copy, "inst"), recursive = TRUE)

Source: tinytest package documentation: setup_tinytest

if (requireNamespace("tinytest", quietly = TRUE)) {
  tinytest::test_package("shelf")
}

[1] "    withr, tinytest"
[1] "CITATION"              "tinytest/test_shelf.R"

Source: tinytest package documentation: test_package

The driver tests/tinytest.R is the three lines printed: it calls tinytest::test_package("shelf") when tinytest is installed. The test files live in inst/tinytest/ and so are installed with the package, which lets a user run tinytest::test_package("shelf") after installation; authors who prefer not to install them can put them in a directory under tests/ and name it in the testdir argument. The grep line shows tinytest added to Suggests (the line is the end of the field). Choose tinytest over testthat when a light dependency matters, when you want the test files to be installed with the package, or when the script style suits the team; the price is the smaller set of expectations, no snapshot tests, no mocking helpers and less tooling around it.

Test coverage with covr

Coverage answers a narrow question: which lines of the package did the tests run? It does not say whether the lines were tested well, only that they were reached, so it finds the code that no test touches and says nothing about the quality of the tests that do. covr (3.6.5, an add-on package) is the standard tool. It modifies the code of the package, adding a tracking call to each call of the source, installs the instrumented copy in a temporary library and runs the tests with it, using tools::testInstalledPackage(). The covr documentation explains why it cannot run inside R CMD check: the modification may change behaviour in edge cases, and for compiled code the package is compiled without optimisation.

Source: covr package documentation: Test coverage for packages

covr::package_coverage() takes the path of the package (the working directory by default) and the type of code to run: "tests" (the default), "vignettes", "examples", "all" or "none". The script runs it on the shelf package and prints the result in the three forms that matter.

cov <- covr::package_coverage()
cov
covr::percent_coverage(cov)

# Lines that no test ran.
covr::zero_coverage(cov)

# Per file, as numbers.
round(covr::coverage_to_list(cov)$filecoverage, 2L)

Source: covr package documentation: package_coverage

shelf Coverage: 93.81%
R/zzz.R: 40.00%
R/loans.R: 96.43%
R/book.R: 100.00%
R/clean.R: 100.00%
R/isbn.R: 100.00%
[1] 93.80531
    filename   functions line value
49 R/loans.R shelf_today   37     0
1    R/zzz.R     .onLoad    2     0
2    R/zzz.R     .onLoad    3     0
3    R/zzz.R     .onLoad    4     0
4    R/zzz.R     .onLoad    5     0
5    R/zzz.R     .onLoad    6     0
6    R/zzz.R     .onLoad    8     0
 R/book.R R/clean.R  R/isbn.R R/loans.R   R/zzz.R
   100.00    100.00    100.00     96.43     40.00

Source: covr package documentation: zero_coverage

The package coverage is 93.81 per cent. The summary lists the files from the least to the most covered: R/zzz.R 40 per cent, R/loans.R 96.43, and 100 for R/book.R, R/clean.R and R/isbn.R. percent_coverage() gives the number (93.80531), and zero_coverage() the lines that no test ran, as a data frame with the file, the function and the line. Two groups of lines are listed. In R/loans.R, line 37 of shelf_today: its body is the one call that reads the clock, and no test runs it, because the tests either pass today explicitly or replace the function with a mock (see Mocking). In R/zzz.R, lines 2 to 6 and line 8 of .onLoad, the package hook that sets the default of the shelf.loan_days option; covr reports that the hook was not run although it runs whenever the package is loaded (the startup message shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days that the hook .onAttach prints is built from the option that .onLoad sets, and it appears in the test log); the cause of the zero was not investigated here, and the number is shown as measured. The last form, coverage_to_list(), gives the same numbers per file for use in code.

The other output formats of covr are for other tools. covr::report() writes an HTML page with the source annotated line by line and opens it, which is the most useful way to work through the uncovered lines. It needs the packages DT and htmltools; DT is not installed in the image used here, and the call fails with the real message below.

# covr::report() writes an HTML report and needs the DT and htmltools packages.
cov <- covr::package_coverage()
tryCatch(covr::report(cov), error = \(e) conditionMessage(e))

Source: covr package documentation: report

[1] "The `DT` and `htmltools` packages must be installed to use `covr::report()`"

Source: covr package documentation: report

covr::codecov() runs the coverage and uploads it to the Codecov service (named here, not run: it needs an upload token, read from the environment variable CODECOV_TOKEN or from a codecov.yml file in the package), and covr has similar functions for Coveralls, GitLab and Azure, and to_cobertura() and to_sonarqube() that write the XML formats other tools read. Lines that should not count, such as defensive branches that cannot be reached, are excluded in the source with the comment # nocov (one line) or a # nocov start and # nocov end pair, by the line_exclusions and function_exclusions arguments of package_coverage(), or with a .covrignore file; the patterns are the options covr.exclude_pattern, covr.exclude_start and covr.exclude_end. A test that should not run under coverage (a slow one, a test of timing) calls skip_on_covr().

Source: covr package documentation: Exclusions

A continuous-integration workflow

Coverage and the checks of the previous sections are usually run on every push by a continuous-integration service. The usethis function use_github_action() copies the maintained workflows of the r-lib/actions repository into .github/workflows/ (use_github_action("check-standard"), use_github_action("test-coverage")), and covr’s own documentation recommends it for setting up coverage. The fragment below shows the shape of such a workflow, with the actions pinned to @v2 and a placeholder package; it is a fragment and was not run, because it needs a hosted runner:

name: R-CMD-check
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
        with:
          use-public-rspm: true
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r-dependencies@v2
        with:
          extra-packages: any::rcmdcheck
          needs: check
      - uses: r-lib/actions/check-r-package@v2

  coverage:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      CODECOV_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CODECOV_TOKEN }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
        with:
          use-public-rspm: true
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r-dependencies@v2
        with:
          extra-packages: any::covr
          needs: coverage
      - name: Test coverage
        run: covr::codecov(quiet = FALSE)
        shell: Rscript {0}

Source: usethis package documentation: use_github_action

Two things in a workflow like this change what the tests see. Continuous-integration services set the environment variable CI (the documentation of skip_on_ci() names GitHub Actions among them), so skip_on_ci() tests skip, and a snapshot that has no stored file is a failure and not a warning (see Snapshots on CI), which is why the snapshot files must be committed. And whether the skip_on_cran() tests run in the R CMD check step depends on whether NOT_CRAN is set in the environment of the job, which the sections above showed to make the difference between SKIP 2 and SKIP 0; read the skip summary in the log, and set NOT_CRAN: true in the env of the job when you want those tests to run. The workflow files themselves were not run here.

Writing code that is easy to test

A test is easy to write when the function under test takes what it needs as arguments and returns what it produces. It is hard to write when the function reads a file, asks for the current date, prints and returns nothing, all in one place. Most techniques of this page (fixtures, mocks, snapshots, skips) exist to cope with code of the second kind, and writing tests is a good way to push code towards the first kind. The shelf package follows this: overdue_loans() takes today, loan_summary() takes today and loan_days, clean_books() and clean_loans() take a data frame and return one, and the code that reads the clock is a one-line internal function.

The script shows the same report written both ways. The first version, report_hard(), reads a file and the clock and prints. The second is three functions: a pure function that counts the loans still out and the late ones from a data frame and a date, a function that formats the counts, and a thin shell that reads the file and prints. The tests then need no file and no clock for the first two, and use the fixed shelf_today of the scenario for the third:

library(testthat)
Sys.setenv(TESTTHAT_EDITION = "3")
set_reporter(StopReporter$new(praise = FALSE))
source("scenario.R")

# The one place that reads the clock.
current_date <- Sys.Date

# Hard to test: it reads a file, asks the clock and prints, all in one place.
report_hard <- function(path = "loans.csv") {
  loans <- read.csv(path, colClasses = "character")
  loans$loan_date <- as.Date(loans$loan_date, format = "%Y-%m-%d")
  out <- current_date() - loans$loan_date[is.na(loans$return_date)]
  cat("Still out:", length(out), "\n")
}

# Easier: a pure function that takes the date and the data as arguments...
count_out <- function(loans, today) {
  still_out <- loans[is.na(loans$return_date), ]
  c(
    out = nrow(still_out),
    late = sum(today - still_out$loan_date > 21L, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}

# ...a function that only formats...
report_line <- function(counts) {
  sprintf("Still out: %d (%d late)", counts[["out"]], counts[["late"]])
}

# ...and a thin shell that does the input and the output.
report <- function(path = "loans.csv", today = current_date()) {
  loans <- read.csv(path, colClasses = "character")
  loans$loan_date <- as.Date(loans$loan_date, format = "%Y-%m-%d")
  loans$return_date <- as.Date(loans$return_date, format = "%Y-%m-%d")
  cat(report_line(count_out(loans, today)), "\n")
}

test_that("count_out() depends only on its arguments", {
  counts <- count_out(
    data.frame(
      loan_date = as.Date(c("2026-06-01", "2026-06-25", "2026-05-01")),
      return_date = as.Date(c(NA, NA, "2026-05-10"))
    ),
    today = shelf_today
  )
  expect_identical(counts, c(out = 2L, late = 1L))
})

test_that("report_line() formats the counts", {
  expect_identical(
    report_line(c(out = 7L, late = 5L)),
    "Still out: 7 (5 late)"
  )
})

test_that("report() works end to end with a fixed date", {
  expect_output(report(today = shelf_today), "Still out: 7 \\(\\d+ late\\)")
})
report(today = shelf_today)
#> Still out: 7 (7 late)

Source: testthat package documentation: Test fixtures

Notice what each test needs. count_out() is tested with a data frame of three rows written in the test, so the expected values (out = 2L, late = 1L) can be checked by reading the test. report_line() is a string function. Only the third test touches the file system and uses expect_output() with a regular expression, because the thin shell has little logic left. The last line prints the same report, Still out: 7 (7 late), for the fixed date.

The habits that follow from this, in the order a reader would meet them:

  • Pass the date, the random seed, the paths and the options as arguments, with defaults that read the real thing (today = shelf_today() in the package), as the test-fixtures article suggests when it says that making external state an explicit argument is often worthwhile because it shows which inputs determine the outputs.

  • Return values and let the caller print. A function that returns a data frame can be tested with expect_equal() and expect_named(); one that only prints needs expect_output() or a snapshot.

  • Keep one idea in a function. The tests in the shelf suite are short because squish(), normalise_isbn() and is_valid_isbn13() are separate functions that can be tested alone.

  • Test the edges, not only the middle. is_valid_isbn13() has a specification for a wrong check digit, a short string, an empty string, NA and a vector of length zero; the loan tests have an impossible date and an early return. The data of the scenario already contain the awkward cases on purpose.

  • When you find a bug, write the test that fails first, then fix it. The test stays as a record. The failure reported in the section on reading a failure (clean_books() of a partial catalogue) is exactly that kind of finding.

  • Test behaviour, not implementation. A test that fixes the exact text of an error message or the exact layout of a print method breaks when those change for good reasons; test the class of the condition where there is one, and use a snapshot, whose diff a human reads, for text that is meant to be read.

  • Do not test R, or other people’s packages. expect_equal(sum(1:3), 6L) tests nothing in your package.

  • Let the file layout help. Name the tests of R/loans.R tests/testthat/test-loans.R; usethis::use_test() (whose template is shown with the layout of the tests directory) creates the file with that name for the active source file, and devtools::test_active_file() runs the test file that goes with the open source file.

The layout of a test suite is also documentation. A new contributor reads the descriptions of the tests as a list of what the code is supposed to do, which is a reason to write them as the sentence "test that …​". The failure reports then read as sentences too: Failure ('test-failing.R:3:3'): overdue_loans() finds 31 late loans.

Common errors and warnings

The messages below were captured while preparing this page; the script that produced the first group is shown, and the others come from the experiments above. It prints the class of the first condition that each statement signals and its message. A mistake in the call of an expectation is usually an error of class rlang_error, with the argument named in backticks, and a mistake in the test code is a failure of the test.

library(testthat)
Sys.setenv(TESTTHAT_EDITION = "3")
source("scenario.R")

# Print the class and the message of the first condition the code signals.
show <- \(code) {
  text <- tryCatch(
    {
      code
      "no condition"
    },
    condition = \(cnd) {
      paste0("<", class(cnd)[[1L]], "> ", conditionMessage(cnd))
    }
  )
  cat(text, "\n", sep = "")
}

# A misspelt argument is a warning, not an error.
show(expect_equal(1, 1, tollerance = 1))
#> <rlang_warning> Unused arguments (tollerance = 1)
# An extra argument of a condition expectation reaches grepl().
show(expect_error(stop("x"), "x", foo = 1))
#> <rlang_error> Failed to compare error to `regexp`.
#> Caused by error in `grepl()`:
#> ! unused argument (foo = 1)
# A forgotten argument.
show(expect_equal(1))
#> <rlang_error> argument `expected` is missing, with no default.
# The description of a test is a single string.
show(test_that(1, expect_true(TRUE)))
#> <rlang_error> `description` must be a single string, not the number 1.
# Arguments are checked: a length must be a whole number.
show(expect_length(1:3, "3"))
#> <rlang_error> `n` must be a whole number, not the string "3".
show(expect_match(1, "a"))
#> <rlang_error> `object` must be a character vector, not the number 1.
# Only editions 2 and 3 exist.
show(local_edition(5))
#> <rlang_error> `x` must be a whole number between 2 and 3, not the number 5.
# A test file that does not exist.
show(test_file("no-such-file.R"))
#> <rlang_error> `path` does not exist.
# A directory without test files.
empty <- file.path(tempdir(), "empty")
dir.create(empty)
show(test_dir(empty))
#> <rlang_error> No test files found.
# Mocking needs to know which package to change.
show(local_mocked_bindings(x = 1))
#> <rlang_error> No packages loaded with pkgload
# Snapshots exist only in the 3rd edition.
show(local({
  local_edition(2)
  expect_snapshot(1)
}))
#> <rlang_error> `expect_snapshot()` requires the 3rd edition.

Source: testthat package documentation: Reference index

Reading them in the order of the output: a misspelt argument of expect_equal() is only a warning (Unused arguments (tollerance = 1)), so the expectation runs with the default tolerance and the typo goes unnoticed in a log full of output; an extra argument of a condition expectation goes to grepl(), which is why the error says that it failed to compare the error to regexp; the message "argument expected is missing, with no default." is the plain R error for an omitted argument; the argument checks of testthat 3.3.0 name the argument and the type that was expected (for expect_length(1:3, "3") the message says that n must be a whole number, not the string "3"); local_mocked_bindings() called with no package loaded by pkgload says so, and a snapshot expectation in the second edition says which edition it needs.

The table adds the messages of the other sections, with the section that explains them.

"there is no package called 'testthat'" in the first line of tests/testthat.R, together with the warning "'library' or 'require' call not declared from: ‘testthat’"

Source: testthat package documentation: testthat 3e

Two of the messages are worth remembering because they are misleading at first sight. Expected ... to throw a error. has the article "a" in front of the word error, as testthat writes it, and the other part of the sentence is the name of the expression that did not fail. And the warning NAs introduced by coercion in a test report is not about the expectation at all: it is the warning of the code that was passed to the expectation, reported against the test that evaluated it, with a backtrace that starts at the expectation.

Pitfalls

The pitfalls below are collected from what the experiments of this page showed. Each is followed by the cure.

  • Testing with expect_true(a == b). When it fails the report says that a == b is not TRUE and nothing else. expect_equal(a, b) and expect_identical(a, b) show both values and the difference. The rule for choosing is that values built by floating-point arithmetic go to expect_equal() and exact things (strings, integers, names, classes) go to expect_identical(). R FAQ 7.31 explains why 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3 to the last bit; 1L and 1 differ for expect_identical() and not for expect_equal().

  • A regular expression where a literal was meant. expect_error(f(), "is.character(title) is not TRUE") treats the parentheses and the dots as regular-expression syntax; add fixed = TRUE (as the shelf test does) or match on class =. Matching on the text of a message also makes the test fragile: the message of an error raised by R or by another package can change between versions and is translated in other languages, and Writing R Extensions advises against testing it.

  • Expecting expect_error() to report that the pattern differed. In the third edition an error that does not match escapes expect_error() and the test reports the original error, with its backtrace (the third failure of the failing-file experiment).

  • A test that depends on the clock, the locale, the time zone, the working directory, the network or a random number. These differ between your laptop and the check machine, which is why the test passes in one and fails in the other. Pass the value in (today = shelf_fixed_today), replace the source with a mock (shelf_today()), fix the state with withr::local_envvar(), withr::local_timezone() or withr::with_seed(), and let the third edition make the output reproducible. Tests that use random numbers need a seed in any case, because R CMD check runs them in a vanilla session without one.

  • State that leaks from one test into the next. An option set with options(), an environment variable, a changed working directory or a file written to the package directory makes the next test, or the next run, depend on this one. Use withr::local_*() and withr::defer(), write only to tempdir() (CRAN Repository Policy: a package should not write in the user’s home filespace, nor anywhere else on the file system apart from the session’s temporary directory, and such usage should be cleaned up), and use set_state_inspector() to find the culprit.

  • Tests that Writing R Extensions lists as bad practice. It names tests of the time a command takes (you cannot know how fast or how loaded the platform is; at best a ratio of times, and even that is not advisable), tests of the exact format of R messages (they change and are translated), tests for the absence of warnings (later versions of R or of other packages can add warnings), comparisons of file paths without canonicalising them (normalizePath()), and numerical tests with no tolerance (only test accuracy after a formal error analysis, and always with a tolerance).

  • Test files that depend on each other. They run in alphabetical order in a serial run, and in an order that depends on which worker is free in a parallel one. Run them with shuffle = TRUE (random order of the top-level expressions in a file) and in parallel now and then to find out.

  • Reading a green check as proof when tests were skipped. SKIP 2 in a check log is two tests that did not run. Look at the skip summary, run the check once with NOT_CRAN=true, and keep skip_on_cran() for tests that are slow or depend on a service, not for tests that are inconvenient.

  • Snapshots accepted without reading. snapshot_accept() makes the new output the truth. Read the diff first. Snapshot only what a human is the judge of, keep the code in a snapshot small, use transform to remove paths, times and versions, and do not snapshot text that other packages or R itself produce (the messages of R change between versions and are translated). Commit tests/testthat/_snaps/, or the tests fail on CI.

  • Relying on a snapshot on CRAN. The snapshot expectations return without checking on CRAN (cran = FALSE), so any behaviour that is checked only by a snapshot is unchecked there. Keep an ordinary expectation for what must hold.

  • Expecting devtools::test() to fail a script. It returns normally when tests fail (stop_on_failure = FALSE). For an exit status, use devtools::test(stop_on_failure = TRUE), testthat::test_local() or R CMD check; test_check() raises an error, and so does test_dir() by default.

  • A test_that() block with no expectation. It is reported as a skipped test, empty test, not as a passing one.

  • Setup that works in test_check() but not in load_all(). Setup files are not sourced by devtools::load_all(). Put what a debugging session needs in a helper file or in the test, and keep the setup file small.

  • Using Sys.setenv() or options() in a test file at the top level, outside a test. The change lasts to the end of the process, not the end of the file, and in parallel runs it persists in the worker. Use withr::local_*() at the top of the file (it lasts to the end of the file) or inside the test.

  • Forgetting that internal functions are visible in tests. Tests run in an environment whose parent is the package namespace, so shelf_today() is visible without :::; the same function from a script outside the package needs shelf:::shelf_today(). Test the exported behaviour first, and write tests of internals only for the logic that needs them.

  • A package used in tests but not declared. Tests that call library(somepackage) or somepackage::fun() for a package missing from DESCRIPTION fail the check (checking for unstated dependencies in ‘tests’), and tests that use a suggested package must be skipped when it is missing. Since testthat 3.3.0 test_that() does the latter on CRAN by itself.

  • Printing noise. A test that prints is hard to read in a log. Use expect_output(), capture.output() or a snapshot, and note that the output of print(), cat() and message() is lost in parallel runs.

Version notes

testthat’s own changes are recorded in its NEWS file (the testthat changelog); the entries below are those that matter for the topics of this page, with the dates of the CRAN releases.

Version CRAN release Change

0.9

2014-09-22

The BDD interface (describe(), it(), in the style of RSpec and Mocha) and skip().

3.0.0

2020-10-31

Editions (Config/testthat/edition: 3, local_edition()); expect_equal() and expect_identical() compare with waldo; condition expectations capture one condition; messages are no longer silenced; snapshot tests (expect_snapshot() and relatives); test fixtures replace setup() and teardown(); test_local(); test_that() sets options to make output reproducible; context(), expect_is(), expect_equivalent(), expect_that(), expect_known_*(), with_mock() and local_mock() deprecated; tests in inst/tests no longer supported.

3.0.3

2021-06-16

The edition can be set by the environment variable TESTTHAT_EDITION; expect_no_match().

3.1.0

2021-10-04

expect_snapshot() is no longer experimental; the variant and transform arguments; in the third edition condition expectations return the condition.

3.1.1

2021-12-03

Condition expectations match across the ancestry of chained errors (inherit); the cnd_class argument of expect_snapshot().

3.1.5

2022-10-08

expect_no_error(), expect_no_warning(), expect_no_message(), expect_no_condition() (experimental until 3.2.0).

3.1.7

2023-03-12

with_mocked_bindings() and local_mocked_bindings() (experimental until 3.2.0).

3.1.8

2023-05-04

it() exported and calls local_test_context(); mocks also bind in the imports namespace and mock S3 methods; the special-files article.

3.1.9

2023-06-15

expect_contains(), expect_in(), is_snapshot(), is_checking(), set_state_inspector(); skip_on_cran() does not skip when run interactively.

3.2.0

2023-10-06

test_file(desc = ); every package uses the snapshot display without condition classes; StopReporter can suppress praise.

3.2.1

2023-12-02

local_mocked_bindings() can mock any object, not only functions; test_file(desc = ) finds describe() tests.

3.2.2

2024-12-10

expect_s7_class(), expect_no_failure(), expect_no_success(), expect_snapshot_failure(); local_reproducible_output() sets LANGUAGE to "C"; with_mock() and local_mock() unconditionally deprecated.

3.3.0

2025-11-13

Requires R 4.1. All failure messages rewritten, and all expectations return their first argument; pass(); expect_all_equal(), expect_all_true(), expect_all_false(), expect_disjoint(), expect_r6_class(), expect_shape(); tests nest arbitrarily; test_that() skips on CRAN when a package it needs is missing; extract_test() and the _problems/ directory; local_mocked_s3_method(), local_mocked_s4_method(), local_mocked_r6_class(); local_on_cran(); shuffle; skip_unless_r(); snapshot_reject() and snapshot_download_gh(); new snapshots fail on CI; SlowReporter; with_mock() and local_mock() defunct.

3.3.1

2025-11-25

The snapshot_download_gh() hint is shown only in a job named R-CMD-check.

3.3.2

2026-01-11

OpenTelemetry traces; LlmReporter; the mock functions for S3 and S4 methods can mock methods that do not exist; test_dir() does not run a single file in parallel.

Source: testthat package documentation: Changelog

The facts about R itself that this page used are these.

R version Change

3.4.0

stopifnot() reports the differences when an argument is a call of all.equal() that is not true.

3.5.0

stopifnot() takes its expressions as exprs.

4.0.0

stopifnot() takes named arguments whose names are the error messages; tools::assertError() and tools::assertWarning() accept a classes argument.

4.1.0

The base environment and its namespace are locked, so bindings can no longer be added to them or removed from them. The native pipe and \(x) lambdas arrive in this release as well; shelf declares Depends: R (>= 4.1.0) because its code uses them, and testthat 3.3.0 requires R 4.1.

4.4.0

The Rd macro \dontdiff{} marks example code whose output is ignored when comparing with reference output, as an alternative to IGNORE_RDIFF comments.

Source: R NEWS: Changes in R 4.0.0, 4.1.0 and 4.4.0 and R NEWS: Changes in R 3.4.0 and 3.5.0

Where older tutorials differ

Many tutorials on testing in R were written for testthat 1.x or 2.x, or for a package workflow of the Travis CI era. They are not wrong about the principle, but several of the functions in them now warn or no longer exist.

Older material says Now See

context("name") at the top of each test file

The file name is the context; context() is deprecated in the third edition

The third edition

expect_is(x, "class")

expect_type(), expect_s3_class(), expect_s4_class(), expect_s7_class(), expect_r6_class()

expect_equivalent(x, y)

expect_equal(x, y, ignore_attr = TRUE)

The third edition

expect_that(x, equals(y)) and is_true()

Plain expectations such as expect_equal(); the old syntax is deprecated and is_true()/is_false() were removed

expect_error(code, NA) to assert that nothing is signalled

expect_no_error() and the other expect_no_*() forms

A first test

The all argument is deprecated; a third-edition expectation captures one condition, so add one expectation for each

expect_snapshot() and expect_snapshot_value(), with the stored results in _snaps/

Where to go next

The package that the tests belong to is built step by step in Creating Packages, and its help pages and vignette in Documentation with Rd, roxygen2 and Vignettes. The next steps of the same workflow are Style, Linting and Static Analysis, which checks the tests as it checks the code, and Publishing to CRAN, which runs the checks that decide whether a package is accepted. For the conditions that tests catch, read Conditions and Error Handling and Defensive Programming and Input Validation; for finding out why a test fails, Debugging. A script that is run from the command line is tested differently from a package, with its exit status as the thing to check: Scripts and the Command Line and, in the section on command-line tools for coding agents, Testing CLIs. The package side of the same topics is in Packages, Libraries and Namespaces (what a namespace is) and S3 Classes and Generics (the book class that the tests exercise). The community book R Packages (second edition) has the chapters Testing basics, Designing your test suite and Advanced testing techniques; the testthat package website has the reference and the articles listed in the references below.
